oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Rav explains that the curses of Parshas Ki Savo hold hidden blessings, just as the bris removes the orlah to reveal the inner holiness of a Jew, and that a father's bris is done purely for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the question of the Zera Kodesh: Parshas Bechukosai ends its curses with consolation, while Parshas Ki Savo ends with curses alone. He notes that at Har Gerizim and Har Eival only the curses are written, and the Gemara learns the blessings from them by a hekesh. He explains that great good is hidden in the Torah, covered by an orlah, and the bris reveals the inner point. Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem es levavcha', is the milah of the year, when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good; this is why Ki Savo is read then. The passuk itself answers: 'these are the words of the bris'. He links the bris to the completion of the child's formation and to Avraham Avinu, and contrasts it with Torah and chuppah, where other motives can enter. A bris is purely for Heaven, and he blesses the child accordingly.

en: Only the curses of Har Eival are written in Ki Savo; the blessings are learned from them by a hekesh, a sign that the blessings are contained within the curses.
Great good is hidden in the Torah under a covering like an orlah; when the orlah is removed, as at a bris, the inner point is revealed.
Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha ve'es levav zarecha', is the bris milah of the year, when the hard months of Tamuz and Av are revealed as good.
The bris completes the formation of the child that began nine months earlier, just as Avraham Avinu with his bris was the completion of creation.
Unlike teaching Torah or arranging a chuppah, where other motives can enter, a father makes a bris purely for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Curses without consolation, and the hidden good

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zera Kodesh's wonder that Ki Savo, unlike Bechukosai, ends without consolation, and notes that only the curses are written while the Gemara learns the blessings from them. He explains that great good lies hidden under an orlah, and that the bris reveals Hashem's covenant with every Jew and the inner point that no place is empty of Him.

title.en: Blessings inside the curses; Elul as the bris of the year

summary.en: Using the hekesh and a rule of Tosafos in Zevachim, the Rav shows that the blessings are contained in the curses. He then explains that Ki Savo is read in Elul because Elul is the milah of the year, hinted in 'umal Hashem', when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good, and compares this to the bris completing a child's formation.

title.en: 'These are the words of the bris' and Avraham Avinu

summary.en: The Rav answers the opening question from the passuk 'eleh divrei habris': the curses are words of the bris, which reveals the inner point. He ties this to the end of the year, to the passuk 'umal Hashem' addressed to the generation of Moshiach and to 'levav zarecha', and to Avraham Avinu, whose holiness flares up at every bris and passes from father to child.

title.en: A bris purely for Heaven, and the blessing

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's list of a father's duties to his son and contrasts Torah study and chuppah, where other motives can enter, as with Elisha ben Avuya's father, with the bris, which a father does with no motive but bringing his child into the covenant of Avraham. He closes with the blessing that just as the child entered the bris, so may he enter into Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the week of Toldos, the Rav contrasts Yaakov's 'today' of Torah and mitzvos with Esav's 'today' of grabbing pleasure, describes the bar mitzvah as the boy's wedding with the Torah attended by his holy ancestors, and calls Toldos, the sixth sedra, a parsha of brachos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yaakov's words to Esav, 'sell me as of today your birthright', and describes two opposite ways of life. The upright Jew's 'today' is 'today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward': Torah and good deeds now, reward later. The rasha's 'today' is 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die': grab the world now. Yaakov told Esav that their 'todays' differ, and Esav answered that he was going to die, so what was the birthright to him. Turning to the bar mitzvah, the Rav says the boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, and brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is celebrated like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah. His holy ancestors come to the simcha, so it must be taken seriously. He speaks of the gifts Hashem gives a bar mitzvah boy, notes that Toldos is a sedra of brachos, and blesses the boy.

en: The Rav describes two opposite views of 'today': the upright Jew's, of doing mitzvos now and receiving reward later, and the rasha's, of grabbing pleasure now.
Yaakov's 'as of today' to Esav expresses that their two 'todays' are opposed.
At bar mitzvah a boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and becomes a chassan to the holy Torah, so the simcha is like a wedding.
The holy ancestors come to a child's simcha, so a bar mitzvah must be treated as a holy occasion, not merely a party.
Toldos is a sedra of brachos and the sixth sedra, which the Rav associates with yesod, the foundation of bracha.

bar mitzvah as a wedding with the Torah
Toldos as a sedra of brachos

title.en: Two kinds of 'today'

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'sell me as of today your birthright' and contrasts the upright Jew's 'today to do them, tomorrow their reward' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'. He then turns to the bar mitzvah boy, who accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and should be a source of nachas.

title.en: A wedding with the Torah, attended by ancestors

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a father must celebrate his son's bar mitzvah like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah, and the holy sefarim that parents and grandparents come from Gan Eden to a child's simcha. Since the boy descends from great tzaddikim, the simcha is a holy occasion and not merely a party.

title.en: Gifts from Hashem and a sedra of brachos

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of giving gifts at a bar mitzvah and says that above all Hashem should give the boy purity of soul and a desire for mitzvos. He notes that Toldos, the sixth sedra, is full of brachos, calls this a good sign, and blesses the boy to become a masmid and a gadol baTorah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Rav ties the mitzvah of milah to the month through the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav", and closes with blessings for the child.

abstract.en: The recording is short and badly garbled, so only the outline can be followed. The Rav brings the passuk from parshas Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav zar'echa", a passuk about milah of the heart, and connects it to the month of Elul; he speaks of a series of pesukim tied to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes the days of Elul, from Rosh Chodesh on, as a preparation for Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year. He returns to the passuk of milah and says this bris took place at an auspicious time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused. He ends with blessings that the child grow up to bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel and be dear before the Ribono shel Olam.

en: The Rav brings the passuk in Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha", in connection with the bris.
He speaks of a series of pesukim that are connected to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li".
The days of Elul lead up to Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year.
The bris took place at a good time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused.
He blesses the child to grow up and bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel.

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha" and ties it to Elul, mentioning a series of pesukim connected to the month, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes Elul as the lead-up to Rosh Hashanah, which sets the whole year.

title.en: A bris in the days of rachamim; blessings

catalogTitle: תיקון לפגם הברית ע"י קר"ש שעל המטה. ביאור בהא דאין אומרים ברכה על דבר איסור.

oneLiner.en: Continuing Tanya chapters 7 and 8, the Rav explains why the sin of wasted seed, though the gravest, can be repaired through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, and why no brachah is made on forbidden food.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews which energies can be elevated and turns to the sin the Shulchan Aruch calls the worst, wasted seed, whose repair is nevertheless close at hand. He explains that both kedushah and klipah have a male and female side, illustrated by the Names Havayah and Adnus, by the numerical value of Amen, and by Yaakov's gift of 580 animals to Esav. Wasted seed is influence without a receiver, so it can be gathered back. In the Sitra Achra the female side is the stronger, which he shows from the Ohr HaChaim's dream and from Rashi on Esav, and he digresses on how the nations follow their angel's left-sided order. He then shows that the repair comes through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, contrasts forbidden relations and a mamzer, speaks of Hashem's ways above the order of judgment, and explains every sin as separation. He closes with Tanya chapter 8 and the Tzemach Tzedek's reason that no brachah is made on forbidden food.

en: Wasted seed is the gravest sin, yet its repair is accessible even now, without waiting for the days of Moshiach or for teshuvah out of love.
Every flow of bounty, in kedushah and in the Sitra Achra alike, needs a giver and a receiver, a male and a female aspect.
Because wasted seed is influence without a receiver, the holy energy thrown to impurity was not absorbed and can be gathered back to kedushah.
The repair comes through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, which the Rav calls the weakest of the daily recitals of Shema and yet the strongest.
Forbidden relations are harder to repair, because the energy is held by the female side of the klipah; a mamzer cannot be undone by the mechanics of teshuvah.
The essence of every sin is separation from Hashem's oneness, and the repair of tumas keri is to believe that nothing is mere chance.
Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rav explains that no brachah is made on forbidden food because a brachah elevates the holy sparks in food, and forbidden food has no ascent.

sin as separation from Hashem's oneness

title.en: Review, and the gravest sin

summary.en: The Rav reviews the previous week: energy from permitted food can later be elevated, while energy from forbidden food cannot. He then introduces wasted seed, called in Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer the worst sin, whose repair is nevertheless available right away.

title.en: Male and female in kedushah and klipah

summary.en: The Rav explains that kedushah has a male aspect, the Name Havayah, and a female aspect, the Name Adnus, whose union is alluded to in Amen; the Sitra Achra has its counterparts. He shows that Yaakov's 580 animals sent to Esav match the numerical value of Esav's force and neutralized it.

title.en: Influence without a receiver

summary.en: The Rav explains that in all forbidden relations there is a giver and a receiver, but wasted seed has no receiver, so it can be gathered back. He tells the Ohr HaChaim's dream of two dogs to show that in the Sitra Achra the female is stronger, and brings Rashi on Esav placing his wives first.

title.en: The nations, their angel, and the left side

summary.en: The Rav digresses: each of the seventy nations is guided by its angel, so the nations put the female first, button left over right and write from left to right, while Jews do the opposite. The Arabs, the refuse of Avraham's chesed, write from right to left and keep a purely lunar calendar, while Jews blend moon and sun with a leap month.

title.en: Teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Tanya: wasted seed can be gathered back through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, the weakest and strongest of the daily Shemas. He notes the Torah never writes it as an explicit prohibition, bringing Rav Tzadok's reason that it is often involuntary, and explains the Gemara that Krias Shema at bedtime is like a double-edged sword against the harmful forces clothed in those drops.

title.en: Forbidden relations and a mamzer

summary.en: The Rav explains that forbidden relations strengthen the klipah more, since the energy is held by its female side, and ordinary teshuvah does not help unless it turns sins into merits. A mamzer cannot be repaired by the mechanics of teshuvah, though the seforim hakedoshim say that through a great teshuvah the mamzer dies and the repair is complete.

title.en: Hashem's ways above the order of judgment

summary.en: The Rav explains the mamzer's death as a release for the suffering neshamah, like a neshamah in a cat, and answers a listener about the future. He then says Hashem is not bound by the order of judgment: at times He purifies a mamzer and keeps him alive, Moshiach comes from such a line, and He will bring the geulah even without teshuvah.

title.en: Every sin is separation

summary.en: Answering a question, the Rav explains that the essence of every sin is separation, as in 'yispardu kol po'alei aven', and that division was created on the second day. Amalek's tumas keri means chance, and he brings Rav Tzadok that its repair is to believe in Hashem's oneness, that nothing simply happens.

title.en: Tanya chapter 8: no brachah on forbidden food

summary.en: Beginning chapter 8, the Rav explains that forbidden food eaten unknowingly for the sake of Heaven still has no ascent, even a rabbinic prohibition. He brings the Tzemach Tzedek that this is why no brachah is made on it, with the Gemara on stolen wheat, the Bnei Yissaschar's inquiry on the brachah over the mann, and the Taz who differs.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Rav explains through the Shem MiShmuel why "a new king arose over Egypt" when milah was neglected, and teaches that tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", bring the bar mitzvah and everyone present a daily renewal in avodas Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Shem MiShmuel, who brings a Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the Jews there not keeping milah, and asks what the connection is. He first brings the Avnei Nezer on a Midrash about Achashverosh's feast: when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, a gift from the Ribono shel Olam, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and that was the feast. The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when the Jews neglected it, Pharaoh seized the "chadash". So too a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which begin with "kadesh li kol bechor": a bechor means newness, and tefillin should renew a person's avodas Hashem every day. The Rav contrasts weekday tefillin with Shabbos tefillin, explains that guests at a bar mitzvah gain renewal and so take back what the new king seized, and closes with blessings.

en: According to the Avnei Nezer, when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and this was Achashverosh's feast.
The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when it was neglected in Egypt, Pharaoh seized the newness, as "a new king arose".
Tefillin open with "kadesh li kol bechor", and bechor means something new; tefillin should give renewal in avodas Hashem every day.
Of all the mitzvos a bar mitzvah becomes obligated in, the main one is tefillin, and the seudah is on account of the tefillin.
Guests at a bar mitzvah recall their own bar mitzvah and gain renewal, taking back what the new king of Egypt seized.

title.en: Why "a new king" arose when milah was neglected

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shem MiShmuel's question on the Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the neglect of milah. Through the Avnei Nezer on Achashverosh's feast he explains that a gift of Hashem left unused is seized by the sitra achra, and so Pharaoh seized the freshness that milah brings.

title.en: Tefillin and renewal at a bar mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", a call to daily renewal in avodas Hashem. He contrasts weekday and Shabbos tefillin, says the guests too gain renewal and take back what the new king seized, and blesses the bar mitzvah and all present.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, the Rav explains that these days and the mitzvah of milah both lift a Jew above nature, drawing down the thirteen middos of rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah: their avodah is not according to nature, and a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun" to a place above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi, where Dovid HaMelech describes the order of nature: at night the animals rule, by day man goes out to his work. In these days a Jew rises at night, against that order. The ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, and the tenth, Yom Kippur, corresponds to "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", the maamar of eating, yet on that very day a Jew rises above nature. Above the sun there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches. According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation; milah too is above nature, and its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos. The child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a sign of yeshuos, and the Rav closes with blessings.

en: The avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature: a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun".
Barchi Nafshi describes nature's order, in which man sleeps at night and works by day; in these days a Jew rises at night against that order.
Yom Kippur, the tenth day, corresponds to the tenth maamar, "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", yet on it a Jew rises above the nature of eating.
Above nature there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches.
According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation, and milah is above nature.
The thirteen brisos of milah correspond to the thirteen middos and draw down rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Rising above nature in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav says the avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi's order of night and day, and explains that the ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, so that Yom Kippur matches the maamar of eating, yet on it a Jew rises above nature.

title.en: Milah above nature; blessings for the child

summary.en: The Rav explains that above the sun is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos. He brings the Maharal that milah, on the eighth day, is above nature, and says its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos; the child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a good sign for Klal Yisroel in these days. He closes by blessing the child to bring nachas to his parents, to Klal Yisroel and to the Ribono shel Olam, and wishes all a gmar chasimah tovah.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in Nissan, the Rav explains that at Pesach daas went out of exile and the Jewish people 'became bar mitzvah', and that a boy becomes a baal daas both by reaching the full measure of daas and by accepting the yoke of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav praises the bar mitzvah boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile and at Pesach it went free, so the Jews came to daas and became, as it were, bar mitzvah. A boy once asked him why he felt no more daas than the day before; the Rav answers that daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or a revi'is, and at thirteen the last drop completes it. This is why the Shabbos before Pesach is Shabbos HaGadol. A second way to become bar mitzvah is like a convert, by accepting the yoke of Heaven, which he ties to 'mishchu u'kchu lachem'. The boy became bar mitzvah on the day of the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together. He closes with the heavenly voice on a bar mitzvah, the gifts one may ask for, and brachos.

en: The Rav brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile, and at Pesach it went out, so the Jews came to daas.
Daas has a fixed measure like a kezayis or a revi'is; at thirteen the boy has its full measure, even if he cannot feel the last drop.
The Shabbos before Pesach is called Shabbos HaGadol because then the Jewish people became 'gedolim', no longer children.
There is a second way to become bar mitzvah, like a convert: by one's will, accepting the yoke of Heaven.
On the day of a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice tells the boy he is born today and may ask for gifts, and he asks for a heart to understand and to know Hashem.

title.en: Daas goes out of exile; the measure of daas

summary.en: The Rav praises the boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the Arizal that at Pesach daas left its exile. He answers a bar mitzvah boy who felt no new daas: daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or revi'is, completed at thirteen.

title.en: Shabbos HaGadol, the convert, and Elyasaf ben De'uel

summary.en: The Rav explains Shabbos HaGadol as the day the Jews became gedolim, and shows a second way of becoming bar mitzvah, like a convert who accepts the yoke of Heaven. He ties the boy's day to the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together.

title.en: Gifts from Heaven, the convert's Pesach, and brachos

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of giving a bar mitzvah boy gifts: a heavenly voice tells him he is born today and may ask, and he asks for a heart to understand and to fear Hashem. He brings the Gemara on a convert and the korban Pesach, and closes with brachos for the boy and his family.

catalogTitle: הסבר על מה שקורא התניא למצוות דרבנן דברי סופרים. חילוק בין שידין נוכראין ושידין יהודאין. עונש דברים בטלים' ומאכלי תאווה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the Tanya calls rabbinic laws 'divrei soferim', how the Chachamim saw the root of every letter of the Torah, and then the Tanya's distinction between non-Jewish and Jewish shedim and the punishments for forbidden food, food of desire and idle talk.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that the Tanya treats a rabbinic prohibition as coming from the klipos, and that it calls the Rabbis 'soferim', after the Gemara that the early sages counted the letters of the Torah. To them every letter was a 'davar shebeminyan', something important in itself, because they saw the root of the Torah; Rabbi Akiva expounded even the crowns of the letters, and Rabbi Meir could write a Megillah by heart because he copied from the Torah's root in heaven. From there he speaks of tzaddikim who read the Torah in the world itself, and of turning the ayin of 'kosnos or' and of the forest swine into an aleph. Returning to Tanya chapter eight, he explains the two kinds of shedim, the severity of chalav akum, two stories about it, and the punishments the sefarim describe for food eaten from desire and for idle talk.

en: The Rav explains that the Tanya holds a rabbinic prohibition draws its life from the klipah, and that the Rabbis know this because they see into the root of things.
He teaches that to the Chachamim each single letter of the Torah was a 'davar shebeminyan', a thing of importance, because every letter taught them new halachos.
Rabbi Meir could write a Megillah by heart because he saw the Torah's root in heaven and was in effect copying from a written text.
The Rav describes the Jew's task as turning the ayin into an aleph: seeing the Master of the world inside what looks like impurity, which sweetens it.

Shedim nukhraim are the desire for forbidden things, while shedim yehudaim are a desire for permitted things that are not needed; the latter can be raised back to holiness through teshuvah or through using the strength for Torah and avodah.
Food eaten only for pleasure leaves a residue even when its strength is used for learning, and the sefarim describe a purging in the grave for it; idle talk brings a different, lighter punishment.

the root of the Torah in heaven
turning the ayin into an aleph
kibbut hakever and the punishment for physical pleasure

title.en: Why rabbinic laws are 'divrei soferim'

summary.en: After a quick review of the text, the Rav notes that the Tanya treats a rabbinic prohibition as coming from the klipah, stresses how precise the Tanya is in every word, and brings the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters. He introduces the idea of a 'davar shebeminyan', using potatoes and oranges to explain it.

title.en: Every letter is a root

summary.en: The Rav explains that ordinary learning needs a phrase that carries a thought, while the Chachamim expounded single letters, and Rabbi Akiva even the crowns on the letters. A letter teaches as the root of a tree feeds its fruit, and the Chachamim could see everything contained in that root.

title.en: Rabbi Meir and reading the Torah in the world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a Sefer Torah may not be written by heart, and asks how Rabbi Meir wrote a Megillah by heart; he answers that Rabbi Meir saw the Torah's root in heaven. Since the world was created through the Torah, tzaddikim could read the Torah in the world, and he tells of a tzaddik who looked at a cut apple every motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Turning the ayin into an aleph

summary.en: From the garments of skin given to Adam and Chava, the Rav explains that the inner point was 'or' with an aleph, light, and that a Jew's work is to turn the ayin into an aleph. He applies this to the suspended ayin in 'chazir miyaar' and to the middle of Tehillim, where the impure can become pure, after a disclaimer that he speaks of matters above his own level.

title.en: Shedim and refined speech

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Tanya: the Rabbis see the root, so they know a rabbinic prohibition comes from the klipos. He reads the Tanya's words that a desire for forbidden food is a shed of the non-Jewish shedim, and explains why refined Jews avoid saying the word 'shed' and speak in refined language, because what a person says is drawn upon him.

title.en: Non-Jewish and Jewish shedim; the Russian censor

summary.en: The Rav defines the two kinds: the shedim nukhraim stir a desire for what is forbidden, while the shedim yehudaim stir a desire for something kosher but unnecessary. Noting that the passage was altered by the censor, he digresses on how Russian censors changed words in seforim, Gemaras and siddurim.

title.en: Why chalav akum is worse than chazir

summary.en: The Rav explains that a desire from the shedim yehudaim can return to holiness through teshuvah or through Torah and avodah, while the shedim nukhraim reach the root of the goy. Therefore chalav akum is in one sense worse than chazir, and he brings the Tzemach Tzedek that chalav akum, chametz on Pesach and niddah touch that root and can block a Jew's readiness for mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The old wine merchant in Tosafos

summary.en: The Rav says that in recent generations people who ate these things lost their readiness for mesiras nefesh. He brings Tosafos' story of an old man who drank wine a goy had touched only to cause him a loss, relying on the ruling that this is not yayin nesech, and who was later killed; the Rav explains that his death al kiddush Hashem showed his ruling was correct.

title.en: Chalav akum, doubts in emunah, and Rav Moshe's milk

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man who complained to the Ba'al HaTanya about doubts in emunah and was told it came from drinking chalav akum. He mentions the dispute over supervised milk in America and tells how Rav Moshe Feinstein, who was lenient for others, vomited up milk without a hechsher served to him. He adds that teshuvah helps, yet until then the thing still tilts toward the other side.

title.en: The residue of food eaten from desire

summary.en: The Rav explains that food eaten only for enjoyment leaves a residue even if one then learns with its strength, comparing it to dust on a mattress that must be beaten out; the musar sefarim call this the beating in the grave, while forbidden food is a real stain that needs the laundering of Gehinnom. Only someone like Rebbi, who had no pleasure from this world, is spared, and he tells of a tzaddik who made a siyum every day so that every meal was a seudas mitzvah.

title.en: The punishment for idle talk

summary.en: The Rav describes a lighter punishment the sefarim give for idle talk, in which the soul is thrown back and forth. He distinguishes the talmid chacham, who is asked why he did not speak words of Torah, from the am haaretz, who is asked why he enjoyed this world, which was made only for the service of Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Succos, the Rav explains why the brachah is made over the lulav, which stands for Yosef the tzaddik, and sees in a bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin a sign for the child.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the four species, which together hold all seven ushpizin: the three hadassim are Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, the two aravos Moshe and Aharon, the lulav Yosef and the esrog Dovid. The Gemara says the brachah is made over the lulav because it is the tallest. He brings the Chasam Sofer's question: the esrog stands for Dovid and malchus, which every brachah mentions, so why not make the brachah over it? The answer is that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia, who earned the name tzaddik through his test, and he reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' as Yosef defending his rank. Under one custom of the order of ushpizin, this day is Yosef's, and a bris, Yosef's mitzvah of guarding the covenant, on his day is no accident but a good sign for the child. He closes with brachos.

en: The four species correspond to the seven ushpizin: hadassim to the Avos, aravos to Moshe and Aharon, the lulav to Yosef and the esrog to Dovid.
The Chasam Sofer asks why the brachah is not made over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus, the theme of every brachah.
The brachah is made over the lulav because it is Yosef, the mashpia, the one who earned the name tzaddik.
In one order of the ushpizin, this day of Succos belongs to Yosef, and a bris on Yosef's day is by Divine providence, not chance.
The bris is the child's first kedushah and brings him into the level of Yosef the tzaddik, a good sign for his future.

title.en: Why the brachah is over the lulav

summary.en: The Rav matches the four species to the seven ushpizin and brings the Chasam Sofer's question why the brachah is not over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus. He answers that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia and tzaddik, and reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' in this light.

title.en: A bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin

summary.en: The Rav notes two orders of the ushpizin, both true; by one custom this day is Yosef's, and a bris meal in the sukkah on Yosef's day, Yosef who excelled in guarding the covenant, is Divine providence and a sign for the child. He closes with brachos for the child and family.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the days of Sefirah, the Rav explains why the heavenly call 'You are My son' comes in the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage': in a world casting off the yoke of Heaven, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'a time for every matter': each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him. In these days before Shavuos the Jews purify themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', newborn, and so too the bar mitzvah boy. He brings from the Zohar that at a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice says 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives new strengths and a yetzer tov; hence the custom of gifts, since He says 'ask of Me and I will give'. He then asks what this has to do with the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal say speaks of the war of Gog and Magog, when the ropes of the yoke of Heaven are torn, as seen in the world today. He answers that once a boy grew up among emunah, but today being a son of Hashem is a great test, so he must, as 'I will tell of the decree' says, keep repeating 'You are My son'. He closes with brachos.

en: Each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him; in the days before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', and so does the bar mitzvah boy.
At a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice proclaims 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives the boy new strengths and a yetzer tov.
The psalm of 'Why do the nations rage' speaks of the time before Moshiach when the yoke of Heaven is cast off, as is seen in the world today.
Once a boy grew up surrounded by emunah; today, exposed to heresy, immodesty and bad middos, being a son of Hashem is a great test.
Therefore, as 'I will tell of the decree' teaches, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem and keep his bar mitzvah day fresh.

title.en: A new offering: the bar mitzvah as a rebirth

summary.en: The Rav ties the bar mitzvah to its season: before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves as a 'new offering' to Hashem, and so does the boy. He brings from the Zohar that a heavenly voice calls 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and explains the custom of bar mitzvah gifts by 'ask of Me and I will give'.

title.en: 'You are My son' in the psalm of Gog and Magog

summary.en: The Rav asks what the bar mitzvah has to do with the psalm 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal apply to the war of Gog and Magog, when the yoke of Heaven is torn off, as he sees in the world today. He contrasts earlier generations, when a boy grew up surrounded by emunah, with today, when being a son of Hashem is a great test.

title.en: 'I will tell of the decree': repeating 'You are My son'

summary.en: The Rav reads 'I will tell of the decree' as a law to repeat constantly that one is a child of Hashem and not act like those who go other ways. He tells the boy to keep his bar mitzvah day and its resolutions fresh, brings that the day should be celebrated like a wedding, and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shemini Atzeres, the Rav brings the Sefas Emes that 'give a portion to seven and also to eight' refers both to Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres and to milah on the eighth day, and sees in their meeting a sign for the child.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash on the passuk 'give a portion to seven and also to eight': seven means the seven days of Sukkos, eight means Shemini Atzeres, and it also means milah on the eighth day. The Sefas Emes says both readings are one idea. The three parts of milah correspond to the three years of orlah, which must be removed so that the sign of the bris is revealed. Seven belongs to the world: the seventy bulls of Sukkos are brought for the nations, and seven is the days of creation. Eight, Shemini Atzeres and milah alike, is the private bond of the Jews with Hashem. Since nothing happens by chance, a bris on Shemini Atzeres is a good sign that this is a higher, Shemini Atzeres child. He blesses the family and Klal Yisroel, ties the eighth to the year of yovel, and prays for the geulah.

en: The Midrash reads 'seven and also eight' both as Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres and as milah on the eighth day, and the Sefas Emes says these are one idea.
The three stages of milah correspond to the three years of orlah, which must be removed before the sign of the bris is revealed.
Seven belongs to the world: the bulls of Sukkos are for the nations, while Shemini Atzeres has no connection with them.
Milah on the eighth day, like Shemini Atzeres, is the bond of union between the Jews and Hashem.
Because nothing happens by chance, a bris falling on Shemini Atzeres is a good sign that the child is of a higher kind.

title.en: Seven and eight: Shemini Atzeres and milah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sefas Emes that 'a portion to seven and also to eight' means both Sukkos with Shemini Atzeres and the bris on the eighth day, explains eight as the private bond of the Jews with Hashem, and sees the bris on Shemini Atzeres as a sign for the child. He closes with blessings, a word on the yovel year, and a tefilah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: דברים בטלים - חילוק העונש בין עם הארץ ותלמיד חכם. ביאור גודל חטא של ביטול תורה וביאור ענין חכמת חיצוניות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 8, the Rav explains why bittul Torah and secular wisdom studied for its own sake are graver than idle talk, tracing secular wisdom to the fragments of the Breaking of the Vessels that remain within kelipas nogah.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 8: forbidden speech belongs to the three impure kelipos and needs the 'hot laundry' of Gehinnom. An am ha'aretz who cannot learn and talks idle talk receives only a general punishment; today's irreligious Jews, who were never taught, are anusim and cannot be blamed. A talmid chacham who wastes his time, however, transgresses bittul Torah, which carries its own punishment. The Rav contrasts Torah, learned lishmah, with secular wisdom, permitted only as a means, and explains why studying it for its own sake is worse than talk about baseball: it defiles the faculties of Chabad, not only the middos. Drawing on the Ramchal and the kings of Edom, he traces secular wisdom to the Breaking of the Vessels: fragments of great lights within kelipas nogah, which can be raised to holiness. He ends with the Rambam and Ramban, Torah immunity and the Chazon Ish.

en: An am ha'aretz who cannot learn receives only the general punishment for idle talk, but a talmid chacham who wastes his time transgresses bittul Torah, which has a special punishment of its own.

Torah must be learned lishmah, for its own sake, while secular wisdom is permitted only as a means, such as medicine to heal people or a skill to earn a livelihood, never for the sake of the wisdom itself.
Studying secular wisdom for its own sake is worse than idle talk such as baseball, because idle talk comes from the middos while secular wisdom defiles Chabad, the higher faculties of the soul.
Secular wisdom comes from fragments of Chabad that fell in the Breaking of the Vessels; it belongs to kelipas nogah and can therefore be raised to holiness.
Only those with great Torah attainment, like the Rambam and Ramban, are immune to the harm in secular wisdom and may use it for Torah; the Gedolei Yisrael knew such wisdom from the Torah itself.

title.en: Idle talk: the am ha'aretz and the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav reviews that forbidden speech belongs to the three impure kelipos and needs Gehinnom to cleanse it. He explains that an am ha'aretz who cannot learn is punished only generally, that today's untaught Jews are anusim who cannot be blamed for the delay of the redemption, and that a talmid chacham who talks idly transgresses bittul Torah.

title.en: The special punishment for bittul Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the kaf hakela, where two angels toss the soul back and forth, is not enough to cleanse bittul Torah; it is a positive commandment like others, yet worse, so it has a special punishment beyond the general one. He contrasts the Gehinnom of fire, for active sins that generate heat, with the Gehinnom of snow, for passive failure to do mitzvos.

title.en: Torah lishmah versus secular wisdom as a means

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tanya's distinction: Torah must be learned lishmah and not as a tool, while secular wisdom may be learned only shelo lishmah, for a purpose such as medicine or a livelihood. Learning it to become wise, like the Greek philosophers, is forbidden, and for a talmid chacham it is worse because he could have learned Torah.

title.en: Why secular wisdom is worse than baseball talk

summary.en: The Rav explains why studying secular wisdom is worse than idle talk about baseball. Such talk is empty and comes from a passion in the middos, so it defiles only the middos of the animal soul, whereas wisdom with real substance defiles Chabad, which is above the middos, and the blemish is far greater.

title.en: The Breaking of the Vessels and the kings of Edom

summary.en: Citing the Ramchal in Derech Hashem, the Rav explains that Hashem's light was too great for the vessels, which cracked, and their fragments became the kelipos. He reads the kings of Edom at the end of Vayishlach: of the first seven it says 'he died', while of the eighth, Hadar, it does not, and his wife is named; he illustrates the pattern of giver and receiver with the image of a fern.

title.en: Giver and receiver: fragments of Chabad

summary.en: The Rav explains that all of creation is built on giver and receiver, male and female, in time, space and soul. When the vessels, the receivers, were too small they broke; with Hadar a wife is named, a world with vessels that could receive and endure. The kelipos formed from the earlier worlds come from very great lights, so secular wisdom is the fallen fragments of Chabad.

title.en: Greek wisdom, kelipas nogah and Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav explains that secular wisdom is not from the three impure kelipos but from kelipas nogah, and can be used for good. Greek wisdom was wisdom for its own sake and defiled the 'oils', which are Chabad; its basic principle of not accepting what one cannot understand is fear, not science. Yavan oppressed the Jews in Eretz Yisrael, and Chanukah's mehadrin min hamehadrin relates to Hadar, the eighth king.

title.en: Questions on the purpose of the Breaking

summary.en: Answering listeners' questions, the Rav compares the Breaking of the Vessels to a hava amina in the Gemara, which has holiness even though it is rejected, and says its purpose was to create a world of free choice. The kelipah keeps only a residue of life, which Hashem wants it to have, and he connects this to drinking on Purim; the true reason for the Breaking will be known when Moshiach comes.

title.en: The Tanya's words and the Rambam and Ramban

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's lines that secular wisdom defiles the Chabad of the G-dly soul and is from kelipas nogah, so it can still serve holiness. He explains why the Rambam and Ramban engaged in it, to bring out the beauty of the Torah, and stresses that the Tanya names them because only someone great in Torah is protected from its harm.

title.en: Immunity before approaching secular wisdom

summary.en: The Rav compares the higher, more dangerous kelipah of secular wisdom to the nations whose land is off limits now, since overcoming it needs greater strength than the middos. Only people like the Rambam and Ramban were immunized; even innocent subjects like medicine are taught today mixed with heresy such as evolution, so one must be well prepared.

title.en: Wisdom from the Torah: the Chazon Ish

summary.en: The Rav says the Gedolei Yisrael knew the sciences from the Torah, as the Ramban writes in his introduction, and tells how great neurosurgeons consulted the Chazon Ish, who mapped out brain surgery and said he knew it from the Torah. He closes by answering a listener's question about Hadar, the eighth king.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the week of Shelach, the Rav explains that the celebration is public because the boy now joins the tzibbur, whose holiness comes from the good point in every Jew's heart, and that he becomes a shaliach of Hashem and of Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why a bar mitzvah is celebrated publicly. A chuppah joins families, and he heard from Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky that this is also why a kiddush is made for a newborn girl; but a bar mitzvah seems to be the boy's private bond with Hashem. He turns to the parsha: the Gemara learns that a davar shebikdusha needs ten from the 'eidah' of the meraglim, and Tosfos wonders why holiness is learned from the meraglim. The Rav explains that every Jew has a point in his heart no evil reaches; ten such points join into a holy whole, since combining exists only in good. A bar mitzvah boy can now complete a minyan, so his simcha belongs to the tzibbur. From Shelach he adds that every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem, and blesses the boy to be a faithful shaliach for Hashem and Klal Yisroel.

en: A chuppah, and a kiddush for a newborn girl, have a social side of joining families, but a bar mitzvah seems to be only the boy's own bond with Hashem.
The Gemara learns that a davar shebikdusha needs ten from the 'eidah' of the meraglim, and Tosfos wonders why holiness is derived from them.
Every Jew has a point in his heart that no evil reaches, and ten such points join together into a holy whole.
Joining together exists only in good, not in evil.
A bar mitzvah boy can now join a minyan and becomes part of the tzibbur, so his simcha is not a private matter.
Every Jew is sent into the world as a shaliach of Hashem and must be a faithful and successful one, like Kalev and Pinchas and unlike the meraglim.

candidateTopics: the good point in every Jewish heart

title.en: Why celebrate a bar mitzvah publicly?

summary.en: The Rav asks why a bar mitzvah, unlike a chuppah that joins families, is celebrated publicly, citing Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky on the kiddush for a newborn girl. He then brings the Gemara that learns the minyan for a davar shebikdusha from the meraglim, and Tosfos's wonder at this.

title.en: The point in every heart joins the tzibbur

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew has a point in his heart no evil reaches, and ten such points, even of people who are not tzaddikim, join into a holy whole, since combining exists only in good. A bar mitzvah boy can now complete a minyan, so the tzibbur gains a new power of good and the simcha is public.

title.en: Shelach: becoming a faithful shaliach

summary.en: The Rav adds that at bar mitzvah the boy becomes fit to be a shaliach, and from parshas Shelach contrasts the meraglim, who failed in their mission, with Kalev and Pinchas. Every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem, and he blesses the boy to fulfill his mission for Hashem and for Klal Yisroel and to bring nachas.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Lech Lecha, the Rav explains that Hashem promised Avraham the land only when he reached Shechem, the place of Yosef and of the bris, because Eretz Yisroel is earned through bris milah.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that Hashem sent Avraham to a land without naming it, and even after he entered Eretz Yisroel did not reveal it to him; only when Avraham passed through to Shechem, Elon Moreh, did Hashem appear and say 'to your seed I will give this land', and Avraham built a mizbe'ach. The Rav explains that bris milah belongs to Yosef, whose place is Shechem. The Jews merit Eretz Yisroel through bris and Torah, which is why the halacha requires mentioning bris and Torah in the blessing of the land. Parshas Lech Lecha is the parsha of bris milah, and Eretz Yisroel is the source of all good flowing to the world. He adds that Shechem is also where Yosef was taken and the first galus began, so the promise there assures the Jews will return. He blesses the family and prays for the geulah.

en: Hashem did not reveal to Avraham that this was the land until he reached Shechem, Elon Moreh, and only there promised it to his seed.
Bris milah belongs to Yosef, and Yosef's place is Shechem.
The Jews merit Eretz Yisroel through bris and Torah, which is why bris and Torah are mentioned in the blessing of the land.
Eretz Yisroel is the source from which all good influence flows to the whole world.
Shechem is also where Yosef was taken and the first galus began, so the promise given there assures the Jews of Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Shechem, the bris and Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem promised Avraham the land only at Shechem, and answers that Shechem is Yosef's place, the place of the bris, through which the Jews merit Eretz Yisroel, as the blessing of the land shows. He adds that Shechem is where the first galus began, and closes with blessings for the family and for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 9, the Rav explains that desires rise from the heart's left chamber to the mind while holiness starts in the mind and comes down to the heart, and that the two souls wage war like two kings over the small city of the body.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the two inclinations and reads Tanya chapter 9: the animal soul sits in the blood of the heart's left chamber. With the example of a person who sees an ice cream, he shows that desire begins in the heart and sends the mind to carry it out, while love and fear of Hashem must begin with the mind contemplating Hashem's greatness and only then move the heart. He supports this from the contrast between David speaking to his heart and Haman speaking in his heart, and explains the prohibition of blood as not strengthening one's own animal soul. He then shows the same order in the blessings before Krias Shema, discusses why the Tanya places anger last and how rarely anger is truly for Heaven, and describes the war of the two kings over the body, with Avraham and the four kings and the war against chametz. He ends with the godly soul's wish to rule alone and the pleasure that lies in the mind.

en: The animal soul and the yetzer hara are seated in the blood of the heart's left chamber, which carries the body's biological life.
Physical desire starts in the heart and sends a message up to the mind, which only works out how to get what the heart wants.
In holiness the order is reversed: nobody naturally desires to learn or daven, so it must begin with the mind contemplating Hashem's greatness, which then brings love and fear into the heart.
Blood is forbidden even where it is not brought on the altar, because the blood is the soul, and eating it would add to a person's own animal soul.
The two souls are two kings waging war over the body, a small city of 248 inhabitants, each wanting all the limbs to follow its rule.
The godly soul wants to rule alone, with the body as nullified to it as a chariot to its rider, so that not even a passing thought serves the other side.

title.en: The animal soul seated in the left chamber

summary.en: The Rav reviews the godly soul and the yetzer hara and begins Tanya chapter 9: the animal soul is in the heart's left chamber, in the blood that carries biological life. He recalls that the midos are called 'double' since they can serve good or bad, and asks why the intellect is not called so.

title.en: Desire rises from heart to mind

summary.en: With the example of a person who sees an ice cream, the Rav explains that desire starts in the heart and the mind only implements it, while love and fear of Hashem must start with the mind and trickle down to the heart's right chamber. A listener asks about the drive for secular wisdom, and the Rav says most intellectual pursuit comes from pride.

title.en: David's heart, Haman's heart, and the blood

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash contrasting David, who spoke to his heart, with Haman, who spoke in his heart, and Rashi on Beshalach and Yisro, to show that the wicked begin with the heart and the righteous with the mind. He then explains the prohibition of blood: the blood is the soul, and eating it would strengthen one's own animal soul. He wonders why the Tanya changes the order of the midos and leaves it for later.

title.en: The godly soul in the brain

summary.en: Continuing the Tanya, the Rav explains that the desires rise from the heart to the brain only to be implemented, while the godly soul's seat is the brain, which he connects to the tefillin of the head and of the arm. Love of Hashem burns in the right chamber like flames, but it comes from deep thought in the mind, since the mind itself is cold logic.

title.en: The order of the blessings before Shema

summary.en: The Rav shows the same order in davening: the blessing of Yotzer describes the vast creation and the awe of the angels, which brings fear, then Ahavah Rabbah brings love, and only then comes Shema. He brings a remark of the Rebbe Rashab that by Ahavah Rabbah the angels are no longer mentioned, and adds that contemplating Hashem's glory brings joy of the heart.

title.en: Why anger is placed last

summary.en: The Rav suggests that the Tanya, being about avodas Hashem, first lists the midos the mind stimulates for good and puts anger at the end, since anger is rarely a tool for serving Hashem. In a discussion with listeners he says anger purely for Heaven is reserved for very special people, and that anger at others usually hides insecurity or pride in one's own group.

title.en: Two kings and the small city

summary.en: The Rav explains that each of the two powers strives to conquer the other, and reads the body as the small city of Koheles with 248 inhabitants, over which two kings wage war. He links this to Avraham's war with the four kings as the four klipos, and to Pesach, bringing the Radbaz's answer to Tosafos' question why chametz is treated so strictly: chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: The godly soul wants to rule alone

summary.en: The Rav explains the godly soul's wish that all the limbs be under its discipline and nullified to it, like a beast of burden to its owner and, more, like a chariot to its rider. It wants not even a passing thought for the other king, as Edom refused even to let Israel pass through its land.

title.en: Overflowing love and the pleasure of the mind

summary.en: The Rav explains that the intellectual fear and the love that come from the mind should fill the heart's right chamber until it overflows into the left and conquers it, as David did. He describes Ahavah Rabbah and the higher love of delight, whose source is the pleasure of the mind in grasping a deep idea, and discusses with a listener how this differs from the satisfaction of accomplishment, with the example of a man alone on an island.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Rav explains that the bar mitzvah day is a 'wedding day' on which the boy is crowned with a new, higher soul, and that at thirteen it becomes visible which family and tree he comes from.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, at his son's bar mitzvah, expounded the passuk 'Go out and see, daughters of Zion' as referring to the crown the Shechinah gives the bar mitzvah boy, calling the day his wedding day. From this the obligation to make a bar mitzvah celebration entered the Shulchan Aruch and the Magen Avraham. The bride, he explains, is the neshamah yeseirah, a new and higher soul, received like the Shabbos soul as a crown. He then asks why bar mitzvah is at thirteen and why it is learned from Shimon and Levi, 'brothers of Dinah': at thirteen a boy's true nature and family surface, as a leaf shows its tree. Finally he brings the heavenly voice declaring 'You are My son', explains the custom of bar mitzvah gifts as a reflection of heavenly gifts, and addresses the boy about his first tefillin and the value of youth.

en: According to the Midrash the Rav cites, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai read 'on the day of his wedding and the day of his heart's joy' as the bar mitzvah day, when the Shechinah crowns the boy.
The bride of the bar mitzvah 'wedding' is the neshamah yeseirah, a new and higher soul that gives the boy a drive to serve Hashem, received as a crown like the extra soul of Shabbos.
Bar mitzvah at thirteen is learned from Levi being called 'ish' at that age, in the passuk about Shimon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah.
At thirteen a boy's true character and the family he belongs to come to the surface, as Shimon and Levi showed when they stood up for their sister.
Bar mitzvah gifts given below reflect the gifts showered on the boy from Heaven, above all a new and higher soul.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's bar mitzvah and the crown of the soul

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai at his son's bar mitzvah, reading 'Go out and see, daughters of Zion' as the crown the Shechinah gives the boy on his 'wedding day', and notes that the obligation to celebrate entered the Shulchan Aruch. He explains that the bride is the neshamah yeseirah, received like the Shabbos soul as a crown.

title.en: Why thirteen: Shimon and Levi, brothers of Dinah

summary.en: The Rav asks why bar mitzvah is at thirteen and brings the derivation from Levi being called 'ish' in the passuk of Shimon and Levi. He explains, through 'the lads grew up' and the image of a leaf that shows its tree, that at thirteen a boy's true nature and family come out, as Shimon and Levi showed by standing up for their sister.

title.en: The heavenly voice, the gifts, and words to the boy

summary.en: The Rav brings the teaching that on the bar mitzvah day a heavenly voice tells the boy 'You are My son', and asks why a bar mitzvah boy receives gifts like a chosson and kallah; he answers that what is done below reflects the heavenly gifts, above all a new soul. He then addresses the boy about his first tefillin and Elokai Neshama, and tells him that greatness is built by working in the young years.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav explains that Hashem comes to every bris twice: on the day of the milah, when He holds the mohel's hand and Himself signs the bris, and on the third day, to visit and bless.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi on 'Vayeira': on the third day after Avraham's milah, Hashem came to ask after his welfare. Since everything stated about milah is eternal, the same happens at every bris, and Hashem comes twice. The first time is at the bris itself. On the verse 'v'charos imo habris' he explains that Avraham feared he might not perform the milah properly, so Hashem held his hand; so too at every bris Hashem holds the mohel's hand like a scribe holds his pen. A signature must come from its owner, and citing the Zera Kodesh he says Hashem's name is inscribed through the bris, so Hashem Himself signs, as the blessing says 'chasam b'os bris kodesh'. The second time is on the third day. He adds that at a bris everyone present has a share, ties Parshas Chayei Sarah's purchase of Chevron to the place of Avraham's bris, and closes with blessings for the child and family.

en: Because what is said about milah is eternal, Hashem's visit to Avraham on the third day after his milah repeats at every bris.
Hashem comes to a bris twice: at the bris itself and on the third day.
Just as Hashem held Avraham's hand at his bris, He holds the mohel's hand at every bris.
The blessing 'chasam b'os bris kodesh' means Hashem Himself signs the bris, since a signature must come from its owner.
At a bris everyone present has a share, unlike other simchos where only some are honored.

title.en: Hashem comes to every bris twice

summary.en: The Rav starts from Rashi that Hashem visited Avraham on the third day after his milah and explains that this repeats at every bris. Hashem comes at the bris itself, holding the mohel's hand as He held Avraham's and signing the bris Himself, and again on the third day to visit and bless.

title.en: Chevron, a share for all, and blessings

summary.en: The Rav ties Parshas Chayei Sarah's purchase of Chevron and the Me'aras HaMachpela to the place of Avraham's bris, explains that everyone at a bris has a share in it, and closes with blessings for the parents, the family and the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Toldos, the Rav explains that the parsha in which all three Avos are together gives blessing and strength to three generations together: grandfather, father and child.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that the parsha is called Toldos, offspring, because it holds the strength, blessing and flow that pass from parents to children. He brings the story of the Yitav Lev, who sat with his grandfather the Yismach Moshe and his father, when the Yismach Moshe asked that all three generations say Torah, in line with the verse that Torah will not depart from a man's mouth, his children's and his grandchildren's. At this bris, too, three generations are together, grandfather, father and the newborn entering the great mitzvah of milah, with Torah and chesed together. Toldos, he says, is the one parsha where all three Avos are together, from Yaakov's birth until Avraham's passing, and this brings blessing to Klal Yisroel and their children. He closes with a blessing for the family.

en: The parsha is named Toldos because it holds the strength and blessing that pass from parents to children.
When three generations are together, Torah is promised to stay with the family, as the Yismach Moshe showed by having all three say Torah.
At this bris three generations, grandfather, father and child, are together in Torah and chesed.
Toldos is the only parsha in which all three Avos are found together, and this brings blessing to Klal Yisroel and their children.

title.en: Three generations and Parshas Toldos

summary.en: The Rav explains the name Toldos as the blessing passed to children, brings the Yismach Moshe's wish that three generations say Torah together, and ties the three generations at this bris to the one parsha where all three Avos are together, ending with a blessing for the family.

catalogTitle: רצון הנפש האלוקות הוא שהגוף יהיה בטל לה לגמרי. חילוק בין אהבה עזה לאהבה רבה. רצון הפנימי של היצה"ר הוא שיהיה מנוצח.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter nine, the Rav explains that the G-dly soul wants the whole body to be utterly nullified to it, distinguishes strong love (ahavah azah) from great love (ahavah rabbah), and shows that the inner wish of the yetzer hara is to be conquered.

abstract.en: The Rav rereads the end of Tanya chapter nine, opening with the verse in Koheles about a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man: the city is the body, and the two souls are two kings fighting over it. The G-dly soul wants every limb to be nullified to it like a pen to the writer or a chariot to its rider, with mind, heart, speech and action given over to Hashem. He explains that the right chamber of the heart should overflow into the left and transform its desires, and distinguishes passing strong love from great love, a delight felt in the mind itself. He describes tzaddikim whose every word and movement served Hashem, with examples from Daniel, Yosef, Pharaoh's reversed heart, the Satmar Rav, the Arizal and the Maggid. He ends with the Zohar's parable showing that the yetzer hara's inner wish is to be overcome.

en: The small city in Koheles is the body, and the G-dly soul and the animal soul are two kings each fighting to rule it alone.
The G-dly soul wants every limb to be nullified to it without asking why, like a pen to the writer or a chariot to its rider.
Ahavah azah is a strong love that can come and go, while ahavah rabbah fills the heart to the brim so that no room is left for the yetzer hara.
Ahavah rabbah is a delight felt in the mind itself, higher than any feeling of the heart, like the joy of finally grasping a hard idea.
In great tzaddikim even ordinary speech and every movement of the hand were directed to Hashem.
The yetzer hara is in the King's service, and its deep inner wish is that a person master and conquer it.

candidateTopics: bittul of the body to the soul
the yetzer hara's wish to be conquered

title.en: The small city in Koheles

summary.en: The Rav starts the page over and reads the verse in Koheles about a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man whom nobody remembers. He explains that the city is the body and the poor wise man is the good inclination.

title.en: Two kings and the nullified body

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's image of the two souls as two kings warring over the body. The G-dly soul wants every limb nullified to it like a pen to the writer and a chariot to its rider, and the three chambers of the mind filled with understanding of Hashem's greatness that gives birth to fear and love.

title.en: The right chamber overflows into the left

summary.en: The Rav explains the ultimate level: the yetzer hara driven out entirely, so that the love in the right chamber of the heart burns like a flame and overflows into the left chamber, overpowering and transforming its desires into love of Hashem, as in serving Hashem with both inclinations.

title.en: Ahavah azah and ahavah rabbah

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes strong love, which comes and goes, from great love, which fills the heart and leaves no room for the yetzer hara. He explains that usually the mind arouses the heart, but in ahavah rabbah the mind itself feels a delight in grasping Hashem, like the thrill of solving a hard problem, and this transforms all the emotions.

title.en: Tzaddikim who speak only to Hashem

summary.en: The Rav describes tzaddikim who feel no worldly pleasure and whose speech, even to people, is directed to Hashem. He notes that the Tanya is a book for beinonim, who should still know what a tzaddik is, and brings Daniel speaking to the king and Yosef's brothers' plea as words that were really addressed to Hashem, a holy language Pharaoh could not learn.

title.en: Pharaoh's heart was liver

summary.en: The Rav explains how Pharaoh withstood plague after plague: the process ran in reverse, the left chamber overflowing into the right. He brings the Midrash on 'kaved lev Paroh' with the parable of the lion, the donkey and the fox, and explains that the liver is the seat of the yetzer hara, while a tzaddik's heart is a real heart.

title.en: The Satmar Rav: a rasha has no heart

summary.en: The Rav brings a vort he heard from the Satmar Rav on 'all hearts fear You'. He explains that Hashem has no body, but the eye, mouth and heart said of Hashem are powers, and man, made in the image of G-d, has physical organs that are a likeness of them; a rasha's heart and eye do not deserve the name, since they do not do what a heart and eye are for.

title.en: Tzaddikim beyond their generation

summary.en: The Rav returns to the perfect tzaddik whose whole day is bound to Hashem and explains that, though generations decline, sometimes a soul of earlier times is sent down, as with the Arizal, the Ba'al Shem Tov and his talmidim, and even the Vilna Gaon. He tells of the Maggid, who noticed a moved snuffbox and who held his hand still for hours because he found no holy reason to move it.

title.en: The yetzer hara wants to be conquered

summary.en: The Rav explains that the yetzer hara, though the opposite of the G-dly soul, is for a person's good: its inner wish is to be conquered. He brings the Zohar's parable of the king who hired a harlot to test his son, and explains the angel of Esav fighting Yaakov on the night before his turn to sing shirah: his shirah was to be overpowered, just as the sun's shirah is its motion, which is why Yehoshua told it to be silent.

title.en: Questions: a bigger tzaddik, a bigger yetzer

summary.en: Listeners ask questions, partly inaudible, about the decline of the generations and the yetzer hara of a tzaddik. The Rav answers that there must always be a balance, so a bigger tzaddik has a bigger yetzer, until he reaches the level of David, who said his heart was hollow within him.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Vayetzei, the Rav explains why Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda was not: milah shows that a person can perfect himself, which is the path of teshuvah of Yehuda and Moshiach ben David.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that this week's parsha tells of the births of Yehuda and Yosef, the roots of the two Meshichim. Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda was not, though Moshiach ben David is higher. He answers with the Chinuch: milah shows that man is created incomplete and can perfect himself. There are two paths, the tzaddik who never sinned, Yosef, the 'tzaddik yesod olam', and the baal teshuvah, Yehuda, from whom comes David, who taught teshuvah. So Yehuda was born with an orlah, to perfect himself. He then brings a vort that most fruits lose their status when crushed, while grapes and wheat rise to wine and bread. With this he explains why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, consoled Avraham with bread and wine: they show that what is crushed can be raised. He closes with blessings that the child carry both qualities.

en: Yosef, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, was born circumcised, while Yehuda, root of the higher Moshiach ben David, was not.
Following the Chinuch, milah shows that a person is created incomplete and can perfect himself.
Yosef represents the tzaddik who never sinned, and Yehuda, through David, represents teshuvah.
Wine and bread show that what is crushed and worked can be raised to a higher level.
Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, could not show Avraham from milah that one can repair oneself, so he brought bread and wine.

candidateTopics: Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef

title.en: Why Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda not

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yosef, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, was born circumcised while Yehuda, root of the higher Moshiach ben David, was not. With the Chinuch's reason for milah he explains that Yosef is the tzaddik who never sinned, while Yehuda and David stand for teshuvah, a person perfecting himself.

title.en: Malki-tzedek's bread and wine, and blessings

summary.en: The Rav brings a vort that grapes and wheat, unlike other fruits, are raised when crushed into wine and bread. With it he explains that Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, consoled Avraham with bread and wine to show that one can repair oneself, ties this to the two Meshichim, and blesses the child to carry both their qualities.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Vayetzei, the Rav explains that Levi received his name from Hashem at the Kisei HaKavod at his bris, and that the bris carries the whole Torah, which is why shevet Levi is bound to it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that the mitzvah of milah comes while the child is still small, and that compared to the height of this mitzvah all are small; it is the root of all of Yiddishkeit. From the week's parsha he brings the passuk of Levi's naming and the teaching of Chazal that the angels brought Levi up to the Kisei HaKavod (Throne of Glory) and Hashem Himself named him. He asks when this happened and answers: at his bris, when a name is given. At a bris Hashem is present openly, as with Avraham Avinu's bris and 'Vayera elav Hashem'. Bris equals 612 and with milah 613, so the whole Torah comes to a bris. Shevet Levi kept milah in Mitzrayim, which is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim. He closes with brachos for the child named Moshe, from a family of talmidei chachamim.

en: The Rav says that compared to the height of the mitzvah of milah everyone is small, and that it is the root of all of Yiddishkeit.
According to Chazal the angels brought Levi up to the Kisei HaKavod and Hashem named him, and the Rav explains that this was at his bris, where a name is given.
At a bris Hashem is revealed openly, as at Avraham Avinu's bris, where the Torah says 'Vayera elav Hashem'.
The word bris equals 612, and with the mitzvah of milah itself 613, so the bris includes all the mitzvos and the whole Torah comes to it.
Shevet Levi alone kept milah in Mitzrayim, so they are bound to the bris, and that is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim.

candidateTopics: naming a child at the bris

title.en: Levi named at the Kisei HaKavod at his bris

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the height of the mitzvah of milah and brings from the parsha that Hashem named Levi at the Kisei HaKavod, explaining that this happened at his bris. He then shows that Hashem is revealed at a bris, as at Avraham Avinu's, and that bris (612) with milah makes 613, so the whole Torah comes to a bris.

title.en: Shevet Levi, the bris, and brachos for Moshe

summary.en: The Rav explains that shevet Levi kept milah in Mitzrayim, which is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim, and ties Levi to Moshe Rabbeinu and to the child's name Moshe. He closes with brachos for the child, from a family of talmidei chachamim on both sides, and for the parents and grandparents.

catalogTitle: יש צדיק שמדריגתו למעלה מדורו. ביאור חילוק בין צדיק וטוב לו לצדיק ורע לו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 10, the Rav explains the difference between the tzaddik who has transformed his evil into good and the tzaddik in whom a hidden residue of evil remains, and describes the special tzaddikim, above their generation, who no longer have a yetzer hara.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 10 and says that now the Ba'al HaTanya begins answering the questions of chapter one: what are tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. There are tzaddikim with no yetzer hara, like David HaMelech, whose heart was 'chalal', empty. He describes the special tzaddikim sent close to the days of Moshiach, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, who remembered earlier gilgulim, and explains why ordinary people forget: to keep their free choice. Pharaoh lost his choice as a punishment, and a story about Czar Nicholas shows that even a rasha's downfall can serve Hashem. The tzaddik who is not complete drives his evil away, but like David leaving Avimelech, it goes off on its own and can return. The complete tzaddik has transformed his evil and despises worldly pleasure, as the Apter Rav did, except where enjoyment itself is the mitzvah, as with eating matzah.

en: There are tzaddikim who have rendered their yetzer hara null and void; David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', empty of it, and so he no longer had free choice in that sense.

Close to the days of Moshiach Hashem sends exceptional tzaddikim, above the normal descent of the generations, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, to keep Klal Yisrael going.
Ordinary people do not remember their earlier gilgulim so that they keep their free choice; perfect tzaddikim, who live only to guide others, may remember.
The tzaddik who is not complete has driven the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, but it was not transformed; a tiny residue remains, subdued and nullified.
The complete tzaddik's evil has been transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures that are not for the service of Hashem.
The complete tzaddik hates evil for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so filled with love of Hashem that no room is left for any other love.
