the yetzer hara of the incomplete tzaddik
love of Hashem and hatred of evil
Kiddush Hashem through the downfall of resha'im

title.en: Tzaddikim with no yetzer hara

summary.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 10 and says the Ba'al HaTanya now begins answering the questions of chapter one about tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. He explains that some tzaddikim have no yetzer hara, as David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', which means empty, like chillul Shabbos empties Shabbos of its kedushah.

title.en: Exceptional tzaddikim near Moshiach's days

summary.en: The Rav says that although the generations grow smaller, close to Moshiach's days there are tzaddikim beyond the normal descent, like the Arizal, whom Reb Chaim Vital describes as grasping more than the nevi'im. He explains that such people are needed because the state of Klal Yisrael today is so low, and he brings the Ohr HaChaim on falling into the fiftieth gate of impurity.

title.en: Tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim

summary.en: The Rav describes the era of the Ba'al Shem Tov, when great neshamos came down and spoke openly of their earlier gilgulim: the Ohev Yisrael of Apt and the Yismach Moshe, who remembered Matan Torah and the dispute of Korach and told his grandson he had stayed neutral. He adds that Korach was a great man with ruach hakodesh, and mentions Reb Shmelke of Nikolsburg and his brother in Mezritch.

title.en: Why we forget: preserving free choice

summary.en: The Rav explains that ordinary people do not remember earlier gilgulim because their task is to fight the yetzer hara, and remembering would remove their free choice. Perfect tzaddikim have finished their own task and live only to guide others, so they may remember; he laments that today there is no such leadership.

title.en: Pharaoh, Czar Nicholas and the rasha's purpose

summary.en: In reverse, Pharaoh lost his free choice as a punishment he brought on himself. The Rav tells how a tzaddik explained why Czar Nicholas died a natural death: he was too wicked to merit a Kiddush Hashem through his downfall, whereas Pharaoh did merit it. He brings the passuk that even the rasha was created for the day of evil, and contrasts David HaMelech, who sanctified Hashem with his life.

title.en: The tzaddik in whom evil remains

summary.en: The Rav lays out the four levels the Tanya will explain: the complete and incomplete tzaddik and the complete and incomplete rasha. He reads how a person fights until he drives the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, yet it was not transformed; a tiny subdued residue remains, which is the Gemara's tzaddik v'ra lo, and the tzaddik thinks it is gone. He then asks whether the Ba'al HaTanya uses a passuk merely as poetic language.

title.en: Vayegarshehu vayelech: the evil that leaves by itself

summary.en: The Rav explains melitza, using a passuk out of context, and says the Ba'al HaTanya means every word exactly. He tells how David feigned madness before Avimelech, and points to the extra word in the passuk: Avimelech thought he drove David out, but David left of his own will. So too the incomplete tzaddik thinks he has driven out the yetzer hara, but it left on its own and is ready to attack again.

title.en: The complete tzaddik and the Apter Rav's matzah

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the complete tzaddik the evil was transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures not for the service of Hashem. He tells of the Apter Rav, who could eat an entire goose after a feast, yet at the end of his life said all food tasted like dust to him except the matzah of the Seder night.

title.en: Achila means enjoyment: the body feels the mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav suggests that the mitzvah with matzah is achila, which means enjoying the food, and brings a proof that one must eat it with appetite. He adds that enjoyment leaves a mark on the body: the Gemara holds one who is mis'asek with forbidden fats liable because he had pleasure, and on Pesach the body itself is to be sanctified by feeling the mitzvah.

title.en: Two reasons the tzaddik hates evil

summary.en: The Rav explains that every desire comes from the sitra achra, and the complete tzaddik hates it for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so full of love for Hashem that no room remains for another love, as in 'ohavei Hashem sinu ra'. He raises the question of how one can also love a fellow Jew, and answers that one loves the part of G-d in him, so the love is not divided.

title.en: Tachlis sinah: hatred and revulsion

summary.en: The Rav brings David HaMelech's words that he hates the resha'im with utmost hatred and asks Hashem to search his heart, showing that the measure of his love is the measure of his hatred of evil. He distinguishes mius, revulsion felt toward objects, from sinah, hatred of people, and explains that the tzaddik's soul is revolted by evil as the senses are by spoiled food. He stops at the complete tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chevron and Shechem, two of the three places in Eretz Yisroel bought with money, are the places of mitzvas milah, and that the bris had to be acquired with mesiras nefesh, which is why the seudah of a bris is so great a simcha.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that although Hashem gave all of Eretz Yisroel to the Avos, three places were bought with money: Har HaMoriah, the Me'aras HaMachpelah and Shechem. Building on the idea that the whole land is a Sefer Torah, with a halacha written into every piece of it, he explains that Chevron is the place of milah: this is why Mamre, its owner, merited that Hashem revealed Himself in his portion, and why the Machpelah was shown to Avraham on the third day of his milah. Shechem, the burial place of Yosef, is also a place of milah, and its people were the great orlah that had to be removed; all three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, can be seen there. Yosef drew strength from Chevron and Shechem before going into exile. Because the bris is the root of everything, it could not come as a gift: it had to cost money and blood, and the joy of the seudah is the joy of mesiras nefesh.

en: Three places in Eretz Yisroel were bought with money even though the whole land was given to the Avos: Har HaMoriah, the Me'aras HaMachpelah and Shechem.
Every part of Eretz Yisroel has a halacha written into it, and Chevron is the place of mitzvas milah.
The Me'aras HaMachpelah can belong only to one connected to milah, so it was revealed to Avraham in the merit of the simcha of his milah.
Shechem, the place of Yosef, is also a place of milah, and all three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, are seen there.
The bris could not be acquired as a gift; it had to cost money and blood, through mesiras nefesh.
The great simcha of the seudah of a bris is the joy of having given blood for Hashem, and each Jew there accepts to do every mitzvah with mesiras nefesh.

candidateTopics: Eretz Yisroel as a Sefer Torah

title.en: Three places bought; Chevron, the place of milah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that three places were bought with money, and the Gemara that Osniel ben Kenaz restored the forgotten halachos after conquering Kiryat Sefer, explained as owning the land where they were written. From this he explains Rashi that Mamre merited Hashem's revelation in his portion because he owned Chevron, the place of milah.

title.en: The Machpelah revealed in the merit of milah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Avraham was shown the Me'aras HaMachpelah on the third day of his milah, long before Sarah died, and answers that it is the place of milah and belongs only to one connected to milah. He adds the Gemara on Pinchas that a tzaddik is buried in the place of his root, and asks how Shechem, Yosef's burial place, fits.

title.en: Shechem, Yosef and the orlah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that the holiest place holds the greatest orlah, so Shechem, a place of milah, was held by Shechem ben Chamor the Chivi, who could not truly be circumcised. He shows that Yosef's root is in Shechem through Osnas, and that Yosef had to pass through Chevron and Shechem to gain the strength of milah before going down to Mitzrayim.

title.en: Milah, periah and metzitzah in Shechem

summary.en: The Rav explains that metzitzah, though by the plain Gemara a matter of danger, is in the inner meaning part of milah: drawing out the bad even from far and deep places. All three parts of milah appear in Shechem: the people were circumcised, the converts were turned to holiness, and the surrounding nations came to war and were defeated.

title.en: Why the places of milah had to be bought

summary.en: The Rav says that because Chevron and Shechem are the places of milah, the greatest kelipos in Eretz Yisroel are found there before the coming of Moshiach. He explains that although the whole land was a gift to Avraham, Har HaMoriah, Chevron and Shechem needed a strong kinyan with money, because one cannot be sure of these things through a gift alone; they require mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The joy of the bris seudah: mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Rav asks why the seudah of a bris is a greater simcha than other mitzvos, and answers that Avraham acquired the kedushah of the bris with his blood and mesiras nefesh, so the bris had to cost money and blood. He brings a saying of Rebbe Avraham Mordechai of Ger that nothing is reached without mesiras nefesh, and closes with brachos for the child and for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on 19 Kislev, the Rav explains that the power of Yishmael rests on his empty milah, and that a Jewish bris done with joy, in the days leading to Chanukah, helps break that power and bring the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by comparing the week of Chanukah to the week of Tisha b'Av, which has laws of lessening joy. Today, 19 Kislev, is the hilula of the Maggid and the release of the Ba'al haTanya, and She'elos uTeshuvos min haShamayim calls it a day of good tidings. He ties this to the day's news: every nation has a heavenly prince, kings below fall only when their prince falls, and a prince of Yishmael has now fallen. Yishmael's twelve nesi'im are twelve angels, and Chanukah, with its reading of the Nesi'im, breaks them; once the fall begins it continues. Yishmael's whole power is his milah, which according to the Zera Kodesh is an empty milah, so his claim to Eretz Yisroel is empty too. A Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy breaks that power. He closes with Moshe, Eliyahu and Moshiach, the child's name Moshe Eliyahu, and brachos.

en: The Rav argues that just as the week of Tisha b'Av has laws of lessening joy, the week of Chanukah, which begins on 19 Kislev, surely carries joy.
Kings below do not fall unless their prince above falls; the day's news shows that a prince of Yishmael in heaven has fallen.
Chanukah, when the parsha of the Nesi'im is read, breaks the power of Yishmael's twelve nesi'im, and once one falls the others will follow.
The whole power of Yishmael is his milah, and a Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy breaks that power.
The Rav says that today's bris and its preparation, from the shalom zachar on, contributed to the fall of the prince of Yishmael, and in its merit Jews will be helped.
Moshiach is the joining of the souls of Moshe and David, together with Eliyahu, and a child named Moshe Eliyahu is tied to the geulah.

title.en: 19 Kislev, a day of good tidings

summary.en: The Rav compares the week of Chanukah to the week of Tisha b'Av and notes that 19 Kislev is the hilula of the Maggid and the release of the Ba'al haTanya, called a day of good tidings in She'elos uTeshuvos min haShamayim. He turns to the day's news and explains that every nation has a prince above, and kings below fall only when he falls.

title.en: Chanukah and the twelve nesi'im of Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yishmael's twelve nesi'im are twelve angels, and brings the Midrash and Targum Yonasan in Parshas Naso that the offerings of the Chanukas haMizbe'ach break them; this is why the Nesi'im are read on Chanukah. Once the fall of the sitra achra begins it continues, and today a prince of Yishmael has fallen.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah, the bris and Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yishmael's whole power is his milah, which according to the Zera Kodesh is empty, so his claim to Eretz Yisroel is empty too; a Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy, with its preparation, helps break that power. He then brings the Chasam Sofer on Moshe, David and Eliyahu in Moshiach, ties it to the Harachaman prayers and the child's name, Moshe Eliyahu, and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the last day of Chanukah, the Rav blesses the child with the words 'Elokim yechonecha beni', as Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once blessed a child born on Chanukah, that he be a Chanukah child.

abstract.en: The Rav says he only wants to give a brachah. He relates that Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once said to a child born on Chanukah 'Elokim yechonecha beni' (may G-d be gracious to you, my son), wishing that he be a Chanukah child, since the seforim say this passuk alludes to Chanukah. The child at this bris was born on the first day of Chanukah and his bris falls on the last day, so the Rav gives him the same blessing: to be a Chanukah child, a child of dveikus and avodas Hashem, bringing nachas to his parents, to the Ribono shel Olam and to all Jews.

en: Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once blessed a child born on Chanukah with 'Elokim yechonecha beni', wishing that he be a Chanukah child.
The Rav notes that the seforim say the passuk 'Elokim yechonecha beni' alludes to Chanukah.
Since this child was born on the first day of Chanukah and his bris is on the last day, the Rav gives him the same blessing.
He blesses the child with dveikus and avodas Hashem, and that he bring nachas to his parents, to the Ribono shel Olam and to all Jews.

title.en: A brachah for a Chanukah child

summary.en: The Rav relates how Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz blessed a child born on Chanukah with 'Elokim yechonecha beni', and gives the same blessing to this child, born on the first day of Chanukah with his bris on the last, together with wishes for dveikus, avodas Hashem and nachas.

catalogTitle: צדיק ורע לו - עוד יש לו שייכות אל הרע. “ראיתי בני עליה והמה מועטים” - זה צדיק וטוב לו. ביאור ענין יחוד קובהו"ש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapters 10 and 11, the Rav explains the levels of tzaddikim, why the highest are called 'bnei aliyah', the meaning of uniting Hashem with the Shechinah, and the many levels of the 'rasha v'tov lo'.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 10. A tzaddik who never sins but keeps a tiny residue of evil is a 'tzaddik she'eino gamur', and this level divides into countless levels; these are the 18,000 tzaddikim of the Gemara. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's 'bnei aliyah', who are few, transformed their evil into good. The Tanya gives a second reason for the name: they serve only for Hashem's need, not even to quench their own thirst for closeness. The Rav explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and the tzaddik reunites them. He develops the pattern of mashpia and mekabel in creation, the Sitra Achra's temporary snatching of a destined union, Eretz Yisrael, and David and Bathsheba. Then, in chapter 11, he explains the 'rasha v'tov lo', why a thought of sin can be worse than a sin, and the many levels of this rasha.

en: A tzaddik who never sins but still has a dormant trace of evil is a tzaddik she'eino gamur, and the Rav identifies these with the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim.
The 'bnei aliyah' whom Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai called few are those who transformed their evil into good and raised it to holiness.
A second reason for the name is that the bnei aliyah do everything only for Hashem's need, not for themselves, not even to satisfy their own thirst for closeness to Him.
Doing a mitzvah 'l'shem yichud' means uniting the Shechinah dwelling in Klal Yisrael, the kallah, with Hashem, the chassan, and so relieving the Shechinah of its exile.
A 'rasha v'tov lo' is a person whose good is temporarily subordinate to his evil at the moment he sins, but whose strong yetzer tov will bring him to teshuvah.
The rasha v'tov lo has countless levels, from one who slips once in ten years to one who sins several times a day and is full of regret.

title.en: The 18,000 tzaddikim and the few bnei aliyah

summary.en: The Rav reviews the tzaddik gamur and the tzaddik who still carries a dormant trace of evil, whose level divides into countless levels. He brings the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement that the bnei aliyah are few, and resolves them: the 18,000 still have a trace of evil, while Rabbi Shimon had none.

title.en: Turning darkness into light

summary.en: The Rav explains the first reason for the name bnei aliyah: they raise and transform their evil into good. He brings the Zohar about Rabbi Chiya, who could not enter Rabbi Shimon's chamber without having turned darkness into light, and notes that the Tanya, which calls itself a book for beinonim, describes this level only so the reader knows what he is not.

title.en: L'shem yichud: uniting chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Rav describes the tzaddik who does nothing for himself, not even for Gan Eden or his own attachment to the Shechinah, and explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and through mitzvos the tzaddik reunites them and relieves the Shechinah of its exile. He reads 'chassid mitchased im kono' as kindness to Hashem's nest, and explains that acting for oneself would mean ego.

title.en: For Hashem's need, not to quench a thirst

summary.en: Reading the Tanya's text, the Rav explains that the bnei aliyah serve for the need above, not to quench their own thirst for Hashem as in the passuk 'Hoy kol tzamei'. He brings the Tikkunei Zohar on the chassid and the Raya Mehemna's parable of a son who gives his life for his parents, then sums up the two explanations of bnei aliyah and notes that the Tanya's bracketed Kabbalistic passage unites them.

title.en: Mashpia and mekabel throughout creation

summary.en: To explain the yichud, the Rav shows that all of creation comes as giver and receiver, sun and moon, day and night, as a parable for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. The Sitra Achra tries to block this union and at times snatches the kallah away, but only temporarily, like a destined match taken by another, and like Eretz Yisrael, first held by Canaan and then returned to Klal Yisrael.

title.en: David, Bathsheba and the hidden union

summary.en: The Rav explains that David and Bathsheba were the destined match of Adam and Chavah and the true parable of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, from whom Moshiach comes through Shlomo, and that David's desire was spiritual. Asked why it came about in such a roundabout way, he answers that the Satan always tries to block Moshiach's coming, so it is hidden, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can, and he says these pesukim cannot be understood at the surface level.

title.en: Chapter 11: the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Rav reviews the levels learned so far and begins chapter 11 on the rasha v'tov lo: at the moment he sins his good is subordinate to the kelipah in the left chamber of the heart, yet he is no complete rasha, since his yetzer tov remains strong. This too divides into countless levels, the lightest being one whose evil overcomes him only rarely and briefly in a small matter.

title.en: Why a thought of sin is worse than a sin

summary.en: The Rav explains why thoughts of sin can in a sense be worse than the sin itself: thought reaches far higher than speech and action, so it brings impurity into a higher sphere. He illustrates with a grease spot that is nothing on the street but disgraceful in the king's palace, mentions wasting free time that could be used for Torah, and explains that at the moment of such a lapse the person is a rasha v'tov lo until his good prevails.

title.en: Many levels of the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Rav describes a lower rasha v'tov lo who sins several times a day, like one who learns, davens and gives tzedakah but habitually speaks lashon hara, and brings Chazal that reshaim are full of regret. He stresses that no one is sold to the yetzer hara beyond return, and closes that every person has a deep chamber in the heart that is a tzaddik gamur, which truly means 'l'shem yichud'.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Erev Shabbos Chanukah

oneLiner.en: At a bris on erev Shabbos Chanukah, the Rav connects the bris, Chanukah, Shabbos and the child's name Elisha to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, healing and long life, and blesses the family.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that it is erev Shabbos Chanukah, so he will speak briefly. At a bris the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are revealed, and on Chanukah as well, so a bris on Chanukah is a double good. Since it falls on the third day of Chanukah, he links it to one of the attributes of mercy. Shabbos, which is being prepared for, is tied to 'erech', from which come healing and long life. He blesses the child, parents, grandparents and all who take part with the blessing of Eliyahu Hanavi, present at every bris. The child is named Elisha; someone pointed out that Elisha brought healing even to a non-Jew, Naaman, so all the more for Jews. This week's sedra contains a kal vachomer, as Rashi notes, and he cites tzaddikim that the thirteen attributes of mercy parallel the thirteen rules of Torah exegesis, kal vachomer corresponding to 'Keil', chessed. The sandek too stands for chessed. He closes with blessings.

en: At a bris the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are revealed, and also on Chanukah, so a bris on Chanukah is doubly great.
Shabbos is connected to 'erech', the source of healing and long life.
Elisha brought healing even to Naaman, a non-Jew; all the more so will the name bring healing to Jews.
The thirteen attributes of mercy parallel the thirteen rules of Torah exegesis, and kal vachomer corresponds to 'Keil', the attribute of chessed.
The sandek also represents chessed.

title.en: A bris on Chanukah: mercy, healing and the name Elisha

summary.en: The Rav links the bris, the third day of Chanukah and Shabbos to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and to healing, draws a kal vachomer from Elisha healing Naaman, ties kal vachomer to the attribute of chessed, and blesses the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Vayechi, the Rav explains that Yosef served as sandek for the children of Machir ben Menashe and so turned Gilead, a place of the mazal of bloodshed, into the source of Eliyahu, the angel of the bris.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk that the children of Machir ben Menashe were born on Yosef's knees, which many explain to mean that Yosef was their sandek. This is said of no other descendants of Yosef. He brings the Gemara that one born under the mazal of Maadim will be a shedder of blood, such as a mohel. Machir's son was Gilead, and the Gemara says Gilead was a place where murderers were common, a place of Maadim. Yosef, with the holiness of the bris, gave Gilead a tikun so that from there would come Eliyahu HaGiladi, the angel of the bris: the blood of Gilead became the blood of milah. He connects Vayechi, the sedra of Yosef, to bris milah, and ends with blessings that the child grow up a tzaddik and chacham and bring nachas to his parents and grandparents.

en: The children of Machir ben Menashe being born on Yosef's knees is understood to mean that Yosef was their sandek, something said of no other offspring of Yosef.
The Gemara says one born under Maadim will shed blood, and one of the possibilities is a mohel.
Gilead, Machir's son and the region of that name, is a place of Maadim, where murderers were common.
Through serving as sandek, Yosef drew the holiness of milah into Gilead so that Eliyahu HaGiladi, the angel of the bris, would come from there.

title.en: Yosef as sandek and Eliyahu of Gilead

summary.en: The Rav reads the passuk about Machir's children born on Yosef's knees as Yosef being sandek, brings the Gemara on the mazal of Maadim and on Gilead, explains that Yosef made Gilead the source of Eliyahu, angel of the bris, ties Vayechi to milah, and blesses the family.

catalogTitle: רשע וטוב לו - יש לו חרטה אחר העבירות אבל לא עשה תשובה. רשע ורע לו - נשמות שמסר יעקב לעשו - אבל יש להם נקודת יחידה ומצטרפים למנין.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 11, the Rav explains the rasha who still feels regret and the rasha in whom the good has departed, and shows that even the lowest Jew keeps a surrounding holiness that joins him to a minyan and that Purim, especially in Adar Sheni, celebrates.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 11. A rasha v'tov lo sins often, yet the living good in him brings thoughts of regret between his sins, though he lacks the strength to stop; the Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard who rewarded his three sober days with a drink illustrates him. The rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; these are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and the Midrash of the am ha'aretz shows they will return to Yaakov when Moshiach comes. The good in such a person has left its nest but hovers above him as a makif. In a long Purim digression the Rav explains, through Amalek, the tribe of Dan, Haman's silver and the silver hooks of the Mishkan, that Hashem never rejects the Jews outside the camp. He then explains that this makif of Yechidah is why ten reshaim make a minyan, and closes with Adar Sheni, Shushan Purim in Yerushalayim, and questions from the listeners.

en: A rasha v'tov lo still has a living good inclination that brings regret between his sins, but it lacks the strength to make him abandon them.
A rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; he is the counterpart of the tzaddik who never thinks of sinning.
The good that leaves such a person does not abandon him altogether but hovers above him as a makif, a surrounding light, like a bird hovering over its nest.

Above every Jew is a holiness of Yechidah, the fusion of all the souls of Klal Yisrael, that no sin can touch; it is revealed when ten Jews gather, which is why ten reshaim make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not.
Hashem never rejects the Jews whom Amalek and Haman regarded as outcasts, and this is the special joy of Purim, especially in Adar Sheni.

candidateTopics: rasha v'tov lo and rasha v'ra lo
no Jew is rejected by Hashem

title.en: The rasha who still feels regret

summary.en: After finding the place in Tanya chapter 11, the Rav explains that a momentary sinner is a rasha only at that moment, and then describes the rasha v'tov lo who sins often and harshly, yet has thoughts of teshuvah between his sins from the living good in him, without the strength to stop.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard

summary.en: The Rav brings the Slonimer Rebbe's reading of the passuk 'mi yiten tahor mitamei lo echad' with the mashal of a drunkard who stayed sober three days and then rewarded himself with a drink, and applies it to the rasha who has regret but not the strength of a firm 'no'.

title.en: The souls Yaakov sent to Esav

summary.en: The Rav explains that those ruled by the yetzer hara are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and tells the Midrash of an am ha'aretz who taught Rabbi Hoshaya that Esav's kings will return the gift to Moshiach; he explains that this was the am ha'aretz's own portion in the Torah, that these souls will return to Yaakov.

title.en: The rasha v'ra lo and the hovering good

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's description of the rasha v'ra lo, who never has thoughts of teshuvah because the good has left its place in his heart, and explains that it still hovers above him as a makif, like a bird above a nest occupied by a serpent, comparing it to the tzelem Elokim that hovers above a non-Jew.

title.en: Adar, the tribe of Dan and Amalek

summary.en: Turning to the month of Adar, the Rav explains that Adar at the end of the year corresponds to the lowest souls, and recalls that the idol-carrying Jews of the camp of Dan were expelled from the Clouds of Glory and fell to Amalek; Hashem does not forgive Amalek for having no mercy on them, because no Jew is rejected by Him.

title.en: Haman's silver and the hooks of the Mishkan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman's ten thousand talents were meant to cancel the half-shekel of the six hundred thousand, but he did not redeem the surplus that became the silver hooks outside the holiness of the Mishkan, the portion of the rejected Jews; this was the 'parashas hakesef' Mordechai told Esther. He adds that the thirteenth month, Adar Sheni, lies outside the twelve combinations of Hashem's Name, and the Purim miracle happened in it.

title.en: Yechidah and the minyan of ten reshaim

summary.en: The Rav asks why ten reshaim make a minyan while nine tzaddikim cannot, and answers that above every Jew hovers a level of the soul, Kedushas Yisrael or Yechidah, the fusion of all souls in the soul of Yaakov Avinu, that no sin affects; Korach's flaw reached up to Levi but not to Yisrael, and ten Jews together reveal this makif.

title.en: The end of the perek and the Purim of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav reads the last lines of the perek, that even the worst rasha has the makif above him and therefore Chazal say the Shechinah rests on every ten Jews, and returns to the joy of Adar Sheni; he explains that Purim is for the rasha who still has regret, and Shushan Purim of Yerushalayim, a walled city, is for those who have nothing but the makif.

title.en: Questions: the inner point, sukkah and the minyan

summary.en: Answering listeners, the Rav explains that the point in every Jew is truly his, but it comes to expression only as a makif when he davens with a minyan; he compares the makif to the sukkah and says it can become inner on Simchas Torah. He adds that one guards against the contagion of rishus but must still care for the rasha, and that the minyan is learned from Korach's congregation.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Vaera Shovevim

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the Friday of Shovevim in the week of Vaera, the Rav explains that at a bris Hashem shows Himself, as He did to the Avos with the name Keil Shakai, and ties the bris to refuah, the leshonos of geulah and the child's name Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav cites the Ba'al HaTanya that 'Va'eira' in the passuk means 'I appeared', and adds another reading: Hashem shows Himself also to the children, not only to the Avos, at certain times of favor, to one who wants to feel it. At the bris Avraham was told 'I am Keil Shakai', the name of the bris, and the passuk says Hashem appeared to the Avos with that name; so at every bris, even today, Hashem shows Himself. The bris falls on a Friday of Shovevim in Vaera, where the tikun of Shovevim begins. The Zera Kodesh says the plagues were healing for Israel, and the Gemara says refuah is the eighth bracha because milah is on the eighth day. The child is named Yisrael, a name that holds all of Klal Yisrael, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov was named Yisrael. He closes with the blessing of Torah, chuppah and good deeds, and wishes for the geulah.

en: Beyond 'I appeared', 'Va'eira' also means that Hashem shows Himself to the children, not only the Avos, at times of favor, to one who wants to feel it.
Keil Shakai is the name of the bris, so at every bris, even in later generations, Hashem shows Himself.
Refuah is the eighth bracha because milah is on the eighth day, and the plagues of Vaera were healing for Israel.
The name Yisrael includes all of Klal Yisrael, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov carried that name.

title.en: Va'eira: Hashem appears at every bris

summary.en: The Rav reads 'Va'eira' as Hashem showing Himself to the children through the name Keil Shakai of the bris, links the bris on a Friday of Shovevim to refuah and the geulah, explains the child's name Yisrael, and blesses the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris during Shovevim, the Rav explains that milah both draws chassadim onto Klal Yisroel and brings judgment on the nations, and that a bris on a Friday of Shovevim is an especially great tikkun.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a passuk whose first letters and last letters both spell milah, which is rarely found. First letters, he explains, stand for chessed, drawing good onto Klal Yisroel, and last letters for din on the wicked. He shows the same pair in the Exodus, where the plagues struck Mitzrayim and healed the Jews, and in the Megillah: the first letters of Esther's words 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' draw chassadim onto Klal Yisroel, while the last letters of Haman's words draw din onto the nations. Milah has both sides: removing the orlah, and drawing chassadim from Avraham Avinu, which is why it was given as the Jews went into exile. In Shovevim, the time of tikkun, a bris is a great tikkun, since Eliyahu Hanavi is present; on Friday, the main day of Shovevim, all the more. He applies this to the dangers facing Jews today and closes with brachos for the child and family.

en: First letters (rashei teivos) stand for the attribute of chessed toward Klal Yisroel, and last letters (sofei teivos) for the attribute of din on the wicked.
In the Megillah, Esther's words carry Hashem's name in their first letters, drawing chassadim on Klal Yisroel, while Haman's words carry it in their last letters, drawing din on the nations.
Milah contains both aspects: it removes the orlah, and it draws chassadim from Avraham Avinu, the head of chessed, onto the Jews.
Shovevim is a time of tikkun, and a bris is a great tikkun, since Eliyahu Hanavi is present at it.
Friday, the sixth day, is the main day of tikkun in Shovevim, so a bris on a Friday of Shovevim is all the more precious.

candidateTopics: exile and protection from the nations

title.en: Milah in first and last letters

summary.en: The Rav explains that first letters stand for chessed and last letters for din, shows both in the Exodus and the Megillah, and explains that milah removes the orlah and draws chassadim. He then explains why a bris in Shovevim, and especially on a Friday, is a great tikkun.

title.en: Today's need and brachos for the family

summary.en: The Rav says that Jews today, threatened by the nations and surrounded in Eretz Yisroel, need both sides of milah, and that this bris on a Friday of Shovevim, in a family of Torah, avodah and chessed, draws great chassadim. He blesses the parents and grandparents and recalls the man the child is named after.

catalogTitle: האדם נברא ביכולת שישליט המוח על הלב. יש לכל יהודי שורש הנעלם שכולו טוב. שייכות לפורים.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Rav explains that the beinoni's evil is only subdued, not killed: it is silenced during true davening and wakes again afterward, yet his mind always has the power to rule over his heart.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 12 and explains that the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, is what we would call a tzaddik, yet he keeps the potential to sin. Comparing it to the Rambam's testimony of the One Who knows hidden things about a baal teshuvah, he says the term describes a present, resolute condition. An antibiotics analogy shows the difference: the tzaddik killed his yetzer hara, the beinoni only knocked it out. He explains the three judges and why the beinoni still gets full credit. During davening, when a channel is cut upward through Pesukei Dezimra and the brachos of Krias Shema, the beinoni rises like a tzaddik; afterward he falls back, like a dancer landing. Finally, an undesirable thought is no failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after the heart, since the mind was created to rule the heart.

en: The beinoni of Tanya never sins and would seem a tzaddik to us, but his yetzer hara is still alive within him.
Being a beinoni describes a present resolute state, so a later sin does not mean he never was one, and teshuvah restores it.
The tzaddik has killed his yetzer hara, while the beinoni has only knocked it out, so it may revive.
During true davening the beinoni's evil is rendered powerless and he is like a tzaddik, but after davening it awakens again.
Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel up through the obstructions, and the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah.
An undesirable thought is not a failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after one's heart; the sin is only letting it linger.
Every person was created with a mind that can rule his heart, so there is no excuse to say he cannot control his thoughts.

title.en: Who is the beinoni of chapter 12

summary.en: After greeting a new listener, the Rav opens chapter 12 on the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, and explains that we would call him a tzaddik. The real tzaddik, like Dovid HaMelech, has killed the yetzer hara in the left chamber of his heart and replaced it with good.

title.en: A present state, like the Rambam's teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni's yetzer hara is suppressed but still there, and that being a beinoni describes his present resolute condition, as the Rambam says of a baal teshuvah that the One Who knows hidden things testifies about him. An analogy of antibiotics taken for too short a time shows the difference between knocking out the yetzer hara and killing it.

title.en: Rasha, tzaddik v'ra lo and the three judges

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Rav distinguishes the rasha and the tzaddik v'ra lo from the beinoni, then explains the judges: the yetzer hara judges the rasha, the yetzer tov the tzaddik, and both the beinoni. Hashem helps the beinoni, and with the passuk 'Hashem lo ya'azvenu' he explains that at the judgment he still gets full credit.

title.en: No barrier: the beinoni's davening

summary.en: The Rav explains that sins create a barrier between a person and his neshamah, so his thoughts wander in davening; he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word of tefillah is a heichal from which the unworthy are thrown out. The beinoni has no such barrier, so while davening he feels the malachim singing and has the status of a tzaddik.

title.en: A person is where his thought is

summary.en: On the Tanya's 'special times' of davening, the Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, proves it from the halachah of designating a tree as one's Shabbos resting place, which he saw in the Satmar Rav and the Avnei Nezer, and applies it to having Yerushalayim in mind in davening.

title.en: The eis ratzon that moves with the sunrise

summary.en: The Rav asks how an eis ratzon outside Eretz Yisrael can be real when everything follows Eretz Yisrael, noting that the Ramak says those abroad miss out and the Ba'al HaTanya in his Shulchan Aruch disagrees. He explains that Above there is no time, and the eis ratzon formed at sunrise moves along with the sunrise, which is why Shacharis is the main time and needs a long davening with tallis and tefillin.

title.en: Cutting a channel: the order of davening

summary.en: The Rav explains that the air up to Shamayim is full of klipos from people's sins, and Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel through them, as the Arizal reads 'zimra' as cutting. Then the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah, preparing for Shema itself, and the bracha after Shema extends yetzias Mitzrayim, freeing oneself from everything that keeps him from Hashem.

title.en: Rising in davening, falling back after

summary.en: The Rav explains that during genuine davening the beinoni's evil becomes subservient to the good and powerless, since even the body sees its root, as the chayos rise to the level of the serafim. After davening the motor shuts off and he falls back, like Chassidim who dance and rise off the ground only for a moment; the evil wakes again but remains only one judge.

title.en: Undesirable thoughts and 'machshavah mamash'

summary.en: The Rav teaches that an undesirable thought comes from the yetzer hara, not from the person's essence, and is no reason to feel guilty; it is an opportunity for the mitzvah of 'v'lo sasuru', which is transgressed only by letting the thought linger. He explains that the beinoni never lets in a 'machshavah mamash', a fully developed thought.

title.en: The mind rules the heart; Reb Shmelke's dveikus

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mind is the ruler over the heart and every person was created able to hold himself back. He tells of the Rebbe Reb Shmelke, who asked his students to tap him if he lost his dveikus while learning, and explains that Torah learned with dveikus is like tefillah, but the Tanya speaks of tefillah. He ends answering a question about Pesukei Dezimra and the eis ratzon.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Shabbos Shirah

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shabbos Shirah, the Rav explains that Hashem made a Jew's eating into mitzvos that bring kedushah into his body, and that the seudah of a bris is a seudah of geulah, bound up with Eliyahu Hanavi and Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the passuk of the manna, 'bread from heaven', and explains that a person's food becomes his life and part of his flesh and blood; eating matzah means taking geulah into oneself. Since all of life depends on eating, Hashem, wishing to give Jews merit, made mitzvos of every meal: washing, hamotzi, the brachos after it, mayim rishonim and acharonim. The Torah is eternal, so every meal is still bread from heaven, and all a Jew's Torah, tefillah and chessed draw their strength from it. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that a passuk about the manna holds all the letters of the alef-beis. Shabbos and every Yom Tov have their own foods. A bris removes the orlah and is a foretaste of geulah, so Eliyahu Hanavi comes, and its seudah is a seudah of geulah that one may not refuse. He closes on Shabbos Shirah and brachos.

en: Food becomes a person's life and part of his flesh and blood, so eating matzah means taking geulah into oneself.
Because all of life depends on eating, Hashem made mitzvos of every meal: washing, hamotzi, the brachos after eating, mayim rishonim and mayim acharonim.
Since the Torah is eternal, every meal today is also 'bread from heaven', and all of a Jew's words of Torah, tefillah and chessed draw their life from his eating.
Shabbos and every Yom Tov, even Chanukah and Purim, have their own foods, halachos and customs.
A bris is a foretaste of the days of Moshiach, so Eliyahu Hanavi comes to it and its seudah is a seudah of geulah.
The Rav explains through this why the poskim say one should not refuse an invitation to a bris seudah: refusing it is refusing geulah.

candidateTopics: the manna as bread from heaven

title.en: Eating as mitzvah and bread from heaven

summary.en: The Rav explains from the manna and from matzah that food becomes a person's life, that Hashem made mitzvos of every meal, and that every meal is bread from heaven. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the letters of the alef-beis in a passuk of the manna, and the special foods of Shabbos and Yom Tov.

title.en: The bris seudah as a seudah of geulah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a bris removes the orlah and is a foretaste of geulah, which is why Eliyahu Hanavi comes and why one should not refuse its seudah. He says the revelation of Eliyahu depends on the home, connects the bris to Shabbos Shirah, and blesses the child and family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Beshalach, the Rav contrasts the hardened heart that brought the plagues on Egypt with the circumcision of the heart that the bris of the flesh awakens in Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the plagues of Egypt, which were made heavier by an even harsher blow, the hardening of the heart, while from all of it came a great salvation for the Jews. Against that hardened heart he sets the heart a Jew asks for: one inclined to love and fear of Heaven and ready to fulfill the will of the Ribono shel Olam. The parshiyos of this time, and Beshalach in particular, speak of that hardening, and since the Torah is a Torah of life, reading them in their week gives strength to work against it. These are also the weeks of Shovavim, set aside for this. The bris of the flesh, he explains, awakens in Heaven the verse that Hashem will circumcise the heart, removing its covering so that fear of Heaven can enter. He closes with blessings that the child grow into an upright Jew and bring nachas to his family and to all of Klal Yisrael.

en: The plagues of Egypt were compounded by a harsher blow, the hardening of the heart, and from all of it came a great salvation for the Jews.
A Jew asks for a heart inclined to love and fear of Heaven and ready to do the will of the Ribono shel Olam, the opposite of a hardened heart.
Because the Torah is a Torah of life, the week in which Parshas Beshalach is read gives strength to work against hardness of heart.
The bris of the flesh awakens in Heaven the circumcision of the heart, as in the verse that Hashem will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring.
The Rav blesses the child to grow into an upright Jew and bring nachas to his parents, grandparents and all of Klal Yisrael.

candidateTopics: torah as a torah of life

title.en: Hardened heart and circumcised heart

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the hardened heart of the Egypt parshiyos with the heart that serves Hashem, ties the bris in the week of Beshalach and Shovavim to the verse that Hashem will circumcise the heart, and closes with blessings for the child.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos Shirah usually brings only a temporary, 'feminine' salvation, but a bris in its week awakens the light of Moshiach and draws down true lights of the final redemption, as on Shevi'i shel Pesach.

abstract.en: The Rav compares the two days on which the song at the Sea is read: Shevi'i shel Pesach, with the haftarah of Dovid's song, and Shabbos Shirah, with the haftarah of Devorah's song. The reading awakens the time, so on Shevi'i shel Pesach, the day of the miracle itself, great lights of redemption come down, reaching to the third Beis HaMikdash. On Shabbos Shirah there is only the reading, and only a semblance of those lights. He brings Chazal that the song at the Sea is called by a feminine name, while the song of the future is masculine: every redemption until the last was followed by more troubles, like a woman who gives birth again and again, but the last will be once and for all. This is why Devorah's song ends with forty years of quiet, while Dovid's ends with kindness to his anointed forever. Since a bris awakens the aspect of Moshiach, a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah can draw true lights of redemption, and he blesses the child accordingly.

en: Reading the account of a miracle awakens the same lights that came down at the time of the miracle.
On Shevi'i shel Pesach the day of the miracle and the reading join and bring great lights of redemption; on Shabbos Shirah there is only the reading, and only a semblance of those lights.
All redemptions before the last were 'feminine', followed again by troubles, while the final redemption will be 'masculine', once and for all.
This is reflected in the endings of the two haftaros: Devorah's song ends with forty years of quiet, while Dovid's song ends with salvation for his offspring forever.
At a bris the aspect of Moshiach is awakened, so a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah can draw true lights of redemption as on Shevi'i shel Pesach.

title.en: Shevi'i shel Pesach, Shabbos Shirah, and the 'feminine' song

summary.en: The Rav explains that the reading of the song at the Sea awakens its lights, fully on Shevi'i shel Pesach and only in part on Shabbos Shirah, and brings Chazal that past redemptions were 'feminine' and temporary, while the final one will be 'masculine' and permanent.

title.en: The two haftaros and the bris that brings redemption

summary.en: The Rav shows the difference in the endings of the haftaros of Shevi'i shel Pesach and Shabbos Shirah, then explains that a bris awakens the aspect of Moshiach, so a bris in this week draws true lights of redemption, and closes with a blessing for the child.

catalogTitle: ביאור איך הבינוני מנצח נסיונות בין אדם לחבירו. אהבת ה' ואהבת ישראל אחד. פורים וי"ג יו"ט של לך כנוס וכו'.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Rav explains that the Beinoni's mind rules his heart while his hidden love for Hashem lies dormant, shows through the 'tip of the yud' how this innermost point is revealed on Yom Kippur and even more on Purim, and ends with how the Beinoni overcomes ill will toward his fellow Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that in the Beinoni the evil inclination is knocked out but still speaks, and that the mind rules the heart by nature, so even Haman could restrain himself. Since light pushes away darkness, bad thoughts are best displaced with holiness. The Beinoni is still not a tzaddik: his advantage is only in function, while in his core lies a hidden love. Through the Gemara on the Purim decree, the forty lashes reduced to thirty-nine, the Rambam on a forced get and the 'tip of the yud', the Rav shows that sin never reaches the fortieth level, revealed on Yom Kippur, on Purim, and through Mordechai's self-sacrifice. He returns to the Beinoni, whose love sleeps after davening, explains why Tanya omits avak lashon hara, how the Beinoni repels thoughts, and how he answers hostility toward a fellow Jew with kindness, closing with a Chassidic story.

en: In the Beinoni the evil inclination still voices its opinion but is never listened to, because by nature the mind rules over the heart.
The Beinoni's advantage is only in his functioning, his thought, speech and action, not in his essence, which is why he is not called a tzaddik.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem in the depths of his heart, a fortieth level, the 'tip of the yud', that sin never reaches.
The atonement of Yom Kippur, and even more the salvation of Purim, come from this innermost place, opened by self-sacrifice.
A passing thought of sin is not a sin for the Beinoni; pushing it away immediately is a mitzvah.
Between man and his fellow, the Beinoni dismisses any feeling of hostility and does the very opposite, treating the other kindly.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, even in Haman

summary.en: After a garbled opening, the Rav reviews that the Beinoni's evil inclination is knocked out but still speaks, reads that the mind rules the heart by nature, and shows it from Haman restraining himself before Mordechai. Bad thoughts are best displaced with holiness.

title.en: Light over darkness; why only a Beinoni

summary.en: With the candle that drives darkness from a whole room, the Rav explains how holiness pushes away the folly of sin. He then asks why so perfect a person is only called a Beinoni, and answers that his advantage is only in function, not essence, like a dancer who must come down.

title.en: The hidden love and the Purim decree

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the Beinoni's heart lies a hidden, natural love of the G-dly soul. He brings the Gemara where Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says the Jews bowed only outwardly, asks how he knew this, and answers that every Jew has a hidden chamber that protests against sin.

title.en: Forty levels and the tip of the yud

summary.en: The Rav explains that creation and man consist of forty forces, the fortieth being the 'tip of the yud' of Hashem's Name, where no sin reaches. With the Rambam on a get given under duress, he shows that the inner will remains good, so lashes are only thirty-nine.

title.en: Yom Kippur, Amalek and Purim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al HaTanya on 'before Hashem you shall be purified': Yom Kippur atones from the Holy of Holies, above the yud. Amalek is the 'first' of impurity set against it. Purim, he says, is even higher than Yom Kippur, and its intoxication is like anesthesia for those who reach it.

title.en: Esther's fear and Mordechai ben Kish

summary.en: The Rav explains Esther's fear that the Jews had sinned even against the innermost point, which Amalek sought to occupy. Hashem Himself judged by the inner point, and Mordechai, 'ben Kish' who knocked on the gates of mercy, sparked the self-sacrifice that opened them.

title.en: Self-sacrifice opens the hidden chamber

summary.en: The Rav explains that the gates of the Holy of Holies open on Yom Kippur through the fast, which is self-sacrifice, and on Purim through the Jews' self-sacrifice. This hidden love is why even sinners gave their lives rather than worship idols, and why the Jews did not abandon their Jewishness to escape Haman's decree.

title.en: The tzaddik's open love, the Beinoni's dormant love

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the tzaddik, who is himself a Holy of Holies like Aharon, with the Beinoni, whose love glows openly only while davening and lies dormant afterward. He may still feel worldly desires, but never acts on them.

title.en: Thoughts of sin and avak lashon hara

summary.en: The Rav explains why thoughts of sin are worse than the sin, that a passing thought is no sin for the Beinoni who repels it, and why the Tanya mentions only two of the three sins no one escapes daily, leaving out avak lashon hara.

title.en: The imprint of davening repels thoughts

summary.en: The Rav explains that being a Beinoni is a great level, that the imprint of davening and the hidden fear and love help him rule over the heart, and that he pushes a bad thought away with both hands. Impurity rises from heart to mind, but without lingering it bears nothing and dissipates.

title.en: Between man and his fellow: doing the opposite

summary.en: Reading the Tanya on matters between man and his fellow, the Rav explains that the Beinoni dismisses hostility and does the opposite, as Yosef did with his brothers. He tells of the Lechovitcher Rebbe and a Chassid whose competitor opened a store across the street, and answers a listener's objection.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Yisro, the Rav shows that Yisro's meal with the elders was a seudas bris that opened him to Torah, and that Hashem takes up the cause of those who come late, so a bris delayed for the child's health is dear and brings healing.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the verse that Aharon and the elders ate bread with Yisro, explaining that this was a seudas bris, since Yisro had converted. Right after it, the next day, Yisro already added a parsha to the Torah, for Torah enters only one who is circumcised, as Chazal relate about Onkelos. He blesses the child, from a family of Torah, to grow into a talmid chacham. In a second talk he brings a Midrash, cited by the Be'er Mayim Chaim, that Amalek attacked those left outside the Clouds of Glory because they had fallen behind, and Hashem fights for them. Yisro too came late, after the counting of the Omer had begun, and feared he would not be accepted, but Hashem draws the latecomer close. So a bris delayed for the child's health is no lesser bris: it shows how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem and draws down healing for all Jews.

en: The meal at which Aharon and the elders ate with Yisro was a seudas bris, held because Yisro had converted.
Torah does not enter one who is uncircumcised, so right after his bris Yisro merited to add a parsha to the Torah.
Amalek could attack only those who had fallen behind and were left outside the Clouds of Glory, and Moshe sent Yehoshua to fight for them.
Yisro, who came after the counting of the Omer had begun, feared he would not be accepted, but Hashem draws close the one who comes late.
A bris delayed for the child's health is not a lesser bris; it arouses in Heaven the importance of a Jew's body and draws down healing.

title.en: Yisro's seudas bris and the Torah that followed

summary.en: The Rav explains that the meal of Aharon and the elders with Yisro was a seudas bris, after which Yisro immediately added a parsha to the Torah, since Torah enters only one who is circumcised, and blesses the child, from a family of Torah, to become a talmid chacham.

title.en: Amalek, the latecomers, and Yisro

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash cited by the Be'er Mayim Chaim that Amalek attacked those who had fallen behind outside the Clouds of Glory and Hashem fights for them, and explains that Yisro, who came late, feared rejection but was drawn close.

title.en: A delayed bris and the worth of a Jew's body

summary.en: The Rav addresses a bris held late, for the child's health: one might think it a lesser bris, but it shows how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem and draws down healing for all Jews; he closes with blessings.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Adar, the Rav explains with the Chasam Sofer that a Jew's true birth is his bris, which is why Haman knew Moshe Rabbeinu's day of death but not his day of birth.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Haman's joy when the lot fell on Adar: he knew Moshe Rabbeinu died in that month but not that he was born in it. Everyone asks why Haman could work out the one date and not the other. The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's answer: the main birth of a Jewish child is at his bris, when he enters kedushah and gains his bond with Torah, mitzvos and the Ribono shel Olam. Haman counted Moshe's birth from an expected bris on the eighth day, not knowing that Moshe was born already circumcised, so his true birth was on the day he was born. The Rav then notes that the days around a birthday share in it, so a bris held now in Adar, close to the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth and in a month of good fortune, is especially auspicious. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

en: Haman rejoiced that the lot fell on Adar because he knew Moshe Rabbeinu died in it, but he did not know Moshe was also born in it.
According to the Chasam Sofer, the main birth of a Jewish child is at his bris, when he enters kedushah.
Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised, so his bris and his birth were on the same day, which Haman did not know.
The days just before and after a birthday share in it, so a bris now in Adar is close to the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth.

candidateTopics: bris as the true birth of a Jew

title.en: The bris as a Jew's true birth

summary.en: The Rav asks why Haman knew the date of Moshe Rabbeinu's death but not of his birth, and answers with the Chasam Sofer that a Jew's true birth is his bris and Moshe was born circumcised. He ties the present bris in Adar to Moshe Rabbeinu's birth and closes with blessings for the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris around Purim, the Rav explains that Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, appears in the Megillah as Charvona at Haman's downfall, because every bris removes the orlah of the world, and that the true joy of 'sasson' is milah, which lifts a Jew above nature.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Charvona's words about the gallows and the Midrash that Charvona was Eliyahu HaNavi, and asks why Eliyahu appears in the Megillah only there and not by name. He explains that Eliyahu is the angel of the bris, a role he earned when he removed the orlah in the incident of Zimri and was given 'My covenant of peace'. Every bris removes orlah and reveals kedushah throughout creation, until all of it is gone and Moshiach is revealed. When Haman, the orlah of creation, was hanged, Eliyahu came as the angel of the bris. The Rav then brings the Chasam Sofer on the word Megillah and the drashah that 'sasson' is milah: with the Rambam's explanation that milah weakens nature, he explains that true joy is not worldly pleasure but rising above nature in a bond with the Ribono shel Olam. He closes with blessings for the child and for the final redemption.

en: According to the Midrash, Charvona in the Megillah was Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes as the angel of the bris.
Eliyahu became the angel of the bris when he removed the orlah in the incident of Zimri and was given Hashem's covenant of peace.
Every bris removes some of the orlah of the world and reveals kedushah, until all of it is removed and Moshiach is revealed.
Haman's hanging was a removal of the orlah of creation, so Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, appears there.
Chazal's 'sasson is milah' means that true joy comes from milah, which weakens a person's nature and binds him to Hashem, not from passing worldly pleasures.

title.en: Charvona, Eliyahu and the angel of the bris

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Charvona was Eliyahu HaNavi and asks why he appears only there in the Megillah. He explains that Eliyahu is the angel of the bris since the incident of Zimri, that every bris removes orlah from creation, and that Haman's hanging was such a removal; Adar is a time of covenant.

title.en: Sasson is milah: true joy above nature

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer on the word Megillah and the drashah that 'sasson' is milah, and with the Rambam that milah weakens nature he explains that true joy is rising above worldly pleasures to a bond with the Ribono shel Olam. He closes with blessings for the child and for the redemption.

catalogTitle: הקב"ה עוזר לבינוני - “כי יעמוד לימין אביון.” י"ג ביאור מאמר חז"ל "אפ' כל העולם וכו' היה בעיניך כרשע." בינוני כצדיק בעיתות רצון. ביאור ענין עתות רצון.

oneLiner.en: Starting from the beinoni who uproots every grudge against a fellow Jew, the Rav shows how the unity of Klal Yisrael reaches the level of keser on Yom Kippur and Purim, and then begins Tanya chapter thirteen: Hashem is the third judge who helps the beinoni.

abstract.en: The Rav finishes the Tanya's description of the beinoni, who rejects every grudge against another Jew and neutralizes anger with compassion, repaying bad with good as Yosef did with his brothers. He then asks how love for every Jew fits with loving Hashem with the whole heart, and answers that a Jew is a part of G-d and all souls are one. That collective soul, beyond the reach of sin, is keser: Moshe Rabbeinu, the half-shekel, the goral of Yom Kippur and of Purim. Haman drew on the keser of impurity, and Esther's counsel to gather all the Jews answered him with unity, which Purim renews through shared food. After explaining why Yosef tested his brothers, the Rav opens chapter thirteen: in the beinoni both inclinations are judges, and Hashem, the third judge, decides for the good.

en: The beinoni lets no grudge against another Jew settle in his mind; he rejects it and neutralizes it with love of Israel and compassion.
Love for every Jew does not divide the love of Hashem, because a Jew's soul is a part of G-d and all Jewish souls are one.
There is a level, called keser, where all souls fuse into one and no sin reaches; Yom Kippur and Purim, both decided by a goral, come from there.
Haman drew on the keser of impurity, and Esther answered him with unity, gathering all the Jews, which reaches the top of keser in holiness.
In the beinoni both the good and the evil inclination are judges voicing opinions, and Hashem is the third judge who tips the scale toward the good.

candidateTopics: Hashem helps against the yetzer hara

title.en: The beinoni uproots grudges

summary.en: The Rav continues the Tanya's account of the beinoni, who rejects any hatred or grudge against a Jew as soon as it surfaces. He explains that compassion neutralizes anger, and that one should repay those who wronged him with good.

title.en: Yosef's test with his brothers

summary.en: The Zohar learns this from Yosef and his brothers. The Rav cites his father-in-law's explanation that the brothers' enmity was sent from Heaven so that Yosef would be tested whether he would bear a grudge, and that he passed it in their merit.

title.en: Can love be divided?

summary.en: The Rav raises the question that love cannot be divided, so how can one love Hashem with all one's heart and also love every Jew. He answers that a Jew is a part of G-d and all Jews are one soul, and brings a sefer that ties the half-shekel to the skull.

title.en: The collective soul and Moshe Rabbeinu

summary.en: Citing the Noam Elimelech, the Rav describes a height where all souls fuse into one, called Yisrael, which no sin can reach. Moshe Rabbeinu is that collective soul, and the half-shekel and the sockets made from it represent every Jew.

title.en: The goral of Yom Kippur and keser

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that the two goats of Yom Kippur must be equal, and Rav Tzadok's explanation: at times Yaakov and Esav cannot be told apart, and only Hashem knows the hidden root where every Jew is a tzaddik. That level is keser, revealed on Yom Kippur and Purim through a goral.

title.en: Haman, Mordechai and the keser of impurity

summary.en: The Rav explains that Parshandasa is the keser of the klipah and that Haman sought to fight Mordechai's keser of holiness, even preventing him from saying Shema. When Haman rose higher in impurity, Esther's counsel to gather all the Jews answered him with unity, and so he is called the 'binder' of the Jews.

title.en: Purim unity through food

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the unity in Shushan alone with that of all the Jews on Purim. Using the eiruv, where shared food makes people one household, he explains that mishloach manos joins all of Klal Yisrael, just as a grudge spoils Yom Kippur.

title.en: Why Yosef tested his brothers

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav links Yosef to the power of unity and to the month of Adar. He then explains that Yosef pressed his brothers so their suffering would complete the repair of his sale, and that he could not hold back the few more moments needed.

title.en: Hashem, the third judge

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter thirteen, the Rav explains Chazal's saying that in the beinoni both inclinations judge: each voices an opinion, and Hashem, who stands at the right of the needy, is the deciding judge. He brings the Maggid Meisharim on the verse 'Hashem will not leave him in his hand'.
